subtopic: TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF MEMBER FOR LEEDS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF MEMBER FOR LEEDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always a matter of sadness to hon. members when one of their fellow members passes away. In the passing of Hayden Stanton, the late member for Leeds, the house has sustained a heavy loss. Through the years he won the confidence of the people of his area and constituency and occupied positions of public importance and service throughout his life. He became a member of parliament seven years ago, and latterly had been chairman of the standing committee on agriculture.
Hayden Stanton was one of those whom to know was to love. Unobtrusive in demeanour, generous in his sympathies, of high integrity and sound in judgment, he had made a place for himself in the hearts of his fellow members. As a farmer he naturally took a particular interest in agricultural pursuits. His own farm would be an example of an outstanding dairy farm, his specialty being Jersey cattle.
He was a devoted public servant. He had the respect and affection of the house. To his widow and son and daughter, to his grandchildren, I am sure I carry with me the unanimity of the house in extending sympathy at the passing of one who in his day and generation gave of his best to his area, to his county, to his province and to his country.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF MEMBER FOR LEEDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the official opposition I should like to associate myself with the Prime Minister in the words of mourning
which he has expressed concerning the death of another of our members. The hon. member for Leeds had been in this house for a period of seven years. He had been actively and continually interested in matters affecting eastern Ontario and generally, as the Prime Minister has already stated, in matters affecting the country as a whole. Like many of us, he had taken an active interest in municipal politics. He was interested in the board of education in the constituency from which he came and he was devoted, in a special manner, to that industry of eastern Ontario concerned with cheese production.
He was quiet and unassuming, and while he did not take part in the deliberations of this house too often when he did join in them he showed without doubt that he was possessed of a deep knowledge of the matters which interested eastern Ontario in a special manner. I have reference now particularly to power development for industrial purposes, the St. Lawrence seaway and matters affecting the cheese producing industry. He had a fine record of public service.
I should like to extend to his widow, to his son Ralph, to his daughter Mrs. Lattimer and to the members of the family the deep condolences of those of us who sit on this side of the house.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF MEMBER FOR LEEDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we join with the Prime Minister and the hon. member for Laurier in their expressions of sympathy and condolences to Mrs. Stanton and to the Stanton family. We were indeed sorrowed to learn of the passing of a fellow member, Mr. Hayden Stanton. In his years in the house I came to know him well. I always found him co-operative, kindly and prepared to meet all members on a fair and equal basis.
Mr. Stanton held almost all the local offices within the gift of his neighbours and the people in his own municipality and district. He served in the House of Commons since 1953, and in recent times was chairman of the committee on agriculture. Mr. Stanton was extremely active in community and service organizations. Always in parliament he was a champion of the cause of agriculture, the industry in which he took such a well known and active part. We extend with others to Mrs. Stanton and to the family our deepest sympathy at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to add just a word or two to what has been said by the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition. The late Hayden Stanton was my seatmate for the last three years. We had' been very closely associated ever since he came to parliament. We had a great many things in common in our preparation, you might say, for the work here in parliament. subtopic: FEDERAL PROPOSALS

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FEDERAL PROPOSALS
speechtext: In view of inquiries that have been made in the house from time to time, Mr. Speaker, I think hon. members might perhaps be interested in the text of a letter which I wrote on December 6 to Premier Bennett of British Columbia and which contained the proposals of the federal government respecting the financing of the Columbia river development. The letter is not short, but if it is the wish of the house I would be prepared to read it.

subtopic: FEDERAL PROPOSALS
speechtext: Go ahead.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FEDERAL PROPOSALS
speechtext:
The letter reads as follows:
My dear Premier:
I duly received your letter dated October 27 concerning the financing of the Columbia river power development. Your writing of the letter followed our personal discussion of the same subject on October 26.
You will undoubtedly have been advised by now that at the meeting of the Canada-British Columbia policy liaison committee on November 23 and 24, the federal ministers amplified the nature and effect of the federal government's offer as first put forward on February 9, 1960, and confirmed in my letter of April 21. Since the questions in your letter under reply were based on the situation previous to the elaboration made at that meeting, I believe it would be appropriate if I were to repeat the outline of the federal offer here, in order that my answers to your questions may appear in their proper context. Subject to satisfactory agreement on the character and functions of a joint federal-provincial co-ordinating agency, along the lines indicated by federal representatives at the recent Canada-British Columbia policy liaison committee, the federal government would give financial assistance in the following manner:
1.	The government of Canada is prepared, subject to the approval of parliament, to advance one half

of the capital cost of creating the storages necessary to implement the proposed treaty between Canada and the United States for the co-operative development of the Columbia river.
2.	The government of Canada will advance these moneys as an investment in a joint project of Canada and British Columbia which will be self-liquidating.
3.	The government of Canada proposes the creation of a joint entity for the purpose (amongst others) of receiving and advancing the federal government's financial contribution. It is understood that you propose to designate the British Columbia Power Commission as the agency to have physical responsibility on behalf of British Columbia for construction and operation of these projects. Subject to satisfactory agreement between our two governments as to the role and position of the joint entity in safeguarding the obligations of the federal government under the treaty and the interests of the federal government (including such matters as the giving of necessary clearances called for by the treaty, adherence to completion dates as may be agreed in the treaty, Canadian content and employment in construction, etc., and such other matters as are appropriate to be entrusted to the entity), and subject to the approval and authorization of parliament, the joint entity could be authorized to advance the federal moneys for capital costs, to British Columbia Power Commission in accordance with the schedule of construction as contracts are approved.
4.	The financing thus provided by the federal government (or guaranteed, if a guarantee arrangement is agreed to be more suitable) would be looked upon as a joint investment with British Columbia, and be repayable by the operating entity to the joint entity on behalf of the federal government, out of revenues earned from the project after operating costs are met. Since it would be a joint investment, capital repayment out of revenues to the federal government would be in the same proportion to total earnings as the capital contribution by the federal government bears to the total capital contributed to bring the project into operation and would be subject to the same maturity dates and other repayment conditions as were applicable to the capital contributed by the provincial government, or by private investors.
5.	Under this arrangement, it would also be possible for the joint entity to receive and disburse the proportion of the capital to be contributed by British Columbia, if the province wishes to handle it that way. Alternative^, it would be possible for the entity to raise the finances directly from the public, with each government agreeing to guarantee the issue proportionately and to purchase proportionately any part thereof from time to time not taken up by public subscription.
Subject to the foregoing, I would answer your request for information on five precise points as follows:
(1)	and (5). You now inquire as to "the maximum amount which the federal government would be prepared to lend to the B.C. power commission". In our oral discussion on October 26, your question was put in rather different form. You then asked if there would be any strings attached to any loan that the federal government might make and, if the loan were to the B.C. power commission, whether the federal government would wish to have a guarantee by the government of the province and, if so, whether on principal, interest or both. As indicated above and as stated in my letter of April 21, I wish to confirm that the government of Canada is prepared, subject to the approval of parliament, to provide one half of the capital cost of the approved storage required to implement the proposed treaty between Canada

and the United States for the co-operative developments of the Columbia river, as an investment in a joint project of Canada and British Columbia that would be self-liquidating.
(2)	The financing provided or guaranteed by the government of Canada would be recoverable with interest from the revenues earned from the project.
(3)	The precise interest rate to be fixed would depend on the form of financing agreed to, but it would obviously have to bear a direct relation to the rate at which the entity could borrow in the market. With guarantees as suggested above, and in view of the advantageous nature of the project which has been arranged, it should be possible to secure a favourable interest rate. The point to be emphasized is that, on the basis of this concept of a joint investment, there would be no question of an interest charge to the British Columbia government for any investment by the government of Canada. Interest will be paid at the same dates as interest is paid on the capital provided by the provincial government, or to private investors on the bonds guaranteed by the provincial government.
(4)	Until its investment has been recovered by it, the federal government would be entitled to receive a share of the net revenue earned from the project in proportion to its contribution to the total capital contributed by the two governments.
You will appreciate that, apart from answering your specific questions in the context of the elaboration of the federal offer referred to, I have confined myself to a very general outline of the nature of the offer and of the ways in which it could be implemented. We are ready and shall be pleased to discuss the details of these and all other questions pertaining to the financing of the Columbia river project, in which the government of Canada has such an important interest, and express the hope that you may see fit to authorize your government's representatives to discuss these questions at the meeting on December 8 and 9.
Yours sincerely,
Donald M. Fleming.
That completes the letter to the premier of British Columbia. I believe the house is aware that a meeting between the two governments is taking place at the present time in Victoria. At that meeting the federal government is represented by my colleagues the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton).

maintopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN "GLOBE AND MAIL"

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN "GLOBE AND MAIL"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I am told that most people, and I belong to that group, often take the substance of an article when they read the headline. This headline reads "Inflow of U.S. Capital Must be Cut, P.M. Says". Then the article reads:
The heavy inflow of U.S. capital investment into Canada must be cut back to reduce the drain of interest and dividend payments across the border, Prime Minister John Diefenbaker suggested tonight.
Then the article goes on to quote what I said. The quotation is entirely correct:
"Canada must expand its exports to the United States, reduce the demand on national earnings from non-resident investment and resolve the conflict between non-resident corporate interests and the national interest."
I emphasize these words in the statement as quoted:
"We must reduce the demand on national earnings."
I went on to point out that it was most desirable that Canadians, to a greater degree than ever before, should invest in the future of their country. I made no statement at any time in the course of my remarks which would in any way have supported the heading or the first paragraph of the article, and on this occasion I have a transcript of what I said.

maintopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN "GLOBE AND MAIL"
speechtext: I wonder if I might ask the Prime Minister to identify the document to which he has referred.

maintopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN "GLOBE AND MAIL"

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BANK OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I receive numerous letters from various people who discuss, sometimes in vigorous terms, their views in

Inquiries of the Ministry relation to monetary policy in general. Though the hon. gentleman has not been too specific, I take it that the subject to which he refers is a letter or letters which occupied a prominent place in this morning's newspapers. I may say that evidently the press received those letters just about 24 hours before I did.
I received one package of letters in this particular envelope which is before me. It is postmarked Ottawa, December 8, and registered. I received it this morning by special delivery. There are, in all, 14 letters, all in the same form and apparently all from the same stencilled impression. Thirteen of the letters were signed by one person each and one letter was signed by four persons, so that this letter, or these letters, have been signed in all by 17 persons. On inquiry I am informed that four of the signatories are associated with Carleton University, one with St. Francis Xavier University and 12 with the University of Toronto.
Mr. Speaker, this is a free country and I presume that professors of economics have the same right as anyone else to express their views on matters of current interest.
I receive many letters on this subject, and the points of view reflected in such letters are varied; they are not by any means identical. I presume these letters, like others on the subject, will receive the consideration that is due to them. In this present case I must say that while the indictment is rather sweeping, the letter is somewhat lacking in any statement of the grounds of the indictment. I am therefore left in some doubt as to the particular grounds upon which this indictment is based.
There have been oral intimations that further letters may be received on the subject; indeed, this package of letters is accompanied by a note which reads as follows:
The enclosed letter was not to be mailed until as many signatures had been contributed as possible, though in time to reach Ottawa on Saturday, December 10.
Unfortunately the press has somehow obtained knowledge of the letter. Therefore, the letter is sent now and the signatures of those who have not had time to mail them will be sent later.
As this enclosure is not signed or dated, Mr. Speaker, I am not in a position to identify the meaning of "now" but obviously it must have been within the last few days; certainly it was not today.
I think that is about all the information I can give to the house on this interesting communication, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MEASURE TO MODERNIZE DISSOLUTION AND ANNULMENT
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-7, to provide in Canada for the dissolution and the annulment of marriage.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to this bill I have to thank chance for the opportunity to discuss it at the present time. It will be recalled that in the last year we have been very interested in the granting of divorces by parliament, particularly with respect to the problems that have arisen in the investigation and study that we have been able to make in this field.
One problem arises from the fact that some of the provinces of Canada have not availed themselves of the opportunity given to them in 1930 by the passing of the Canada divorce act to set up their own divorce courts. This has resulted in parliament granting divorces upon petition for people residing in the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland. We have objected to the granting of divorces in this way. The other place has a committee which rules on divorce petitions.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MEASURE TO MODERNIZE DISSOLUTION AND ANNULMENT
speechtext: I wonder whether the hon. member would permit me to interrupt for a moment. There seems to be more than the usual conversation which I am not sure is directed to the bill before us. I hope hon. members will reserve it until they get the floor so that we can hear the hon. member for Timiskaming now.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MEASURE TO MODERNIZE DISSOLUTION AND ANNULMENT
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I think some of it is probably directed toward

the introduction of this bill, and I hope to hear from those on the other side during the debate.
We have felt that the House of Commons cannot rule efficiently on divorce petitions, and are concerned about cases of this type and their effect on the work of the house and the other place as well. It seems to me that members of parliament and members of the other place, many of whom were formerly members of parliament or are public spirited citizens, do not have the ability to judge these cases and in most cases they do not have the inclination to act as a judicial body. There is a lack of staff in the house and in the other place to deal properly with the divorce petitions we are asked to pass through the parliament of Canada.
One thing that is surprising and about which we are very concerned, as I think all Canadians are, is that with respect to divorce actions brought before parliament there is no Queen's proctor. When investigations were made in some provinces they were brought about at the instigation and through the efforts of the Queen's proctor. We also find in the House of Commons, as I am sure they do in the other place, that political influence is exerted by members of parliament and members of the other place on individual members to allow a certain dispensation to come about when the person involved in the case is a friend, relation, constituent or other interested party. This would not be tolerated by a court. It happens here because of personal relationships and because there seems to be nothing wrong about doing this so far as these petitions are concerned.
We are also concerned about something that is probably more important than anything else with relation to the granting of divorces by parliament, and that is the question of children and their protection. If we were a duly constituted court we could give full consideration to the custody and maintenance of children. In the House of Commons we are not even allowed to discuss what will happen to the children as the result of a divorce action. We are also not able to afford any protection to the wife particularly so far as property rights and their disposition are concerned.
There is another very important issue, and that is the matter of appeals. In the eyes of the general public and legally speaking, we constitute the highest court of the land, and from this court there can be no appeal. If such conditions exist as have been pointed out many times in the newspapers, then it is not right that there should be no appeal. We might find that a case had been proved to our satisfaction, but if there were a court of appeal our decision might very well be reversed.
Proposed Divorce Measures
Since I first became interested in the question of divorce and the procedure followed in these cases many Canadians have also taken an interest in the matter. The result is the introduction of the bill now before us, which in my opinion will solve many of the problems that now exist with relation to the granting of divorce in Canada.
I	should like to read one or two short articles. The first is a letter that appeared in Liberty magazine last year which in my opinion is nothing but a confession of perjury and collusion. The name of the writer of the letter was withheld, but he lives in Montreal. The letter reads as follows:
I wish to congratulate you on this outspoken article. Eight at the moment, my wife and I are going through this mill, and I do hope that, because of your article, something concrete will be done to clean up this mess.
From the very moment that I paid the $1,200 for the divorce until now, everything about it has been in very poor taste. My wife and I mutually agreed on a divorce, even to the point of paying for it. Later I discovered that I should never have discussed with friends that I paid for the action, because this Is considered collusion.
Later I agreed to meet the detective (in order to avoid having papers served on me at the office) for him to get the ''evidence" on me. The "evidence" consisted of sitting in his office, and discussing, among other things, the "divorce laws" of Quebec, and having a beer, which was served by a female employee. He asked me if I would like to go and meet the girl. I said, "Do I have to?" He said, "No, but you may have to swear that you had relations with her."
Right now, I'm ready to swear that not only did I not have relations with any woman that night, nor have I ever (to my knowledge) talked with or even seen the girl mentioned in the action. If this isn't "collusion", I'd like to know what is.
We are only using this as an example, Mr. Speaker. This court did not even investigate this particular charge, although I am quite sure it was within the power of the Minister of Justice to ask this magazine to divulge the name if he wished to go into the matter to the full extent.
In an article in the Globe and Mail dated July 23, 1960, there is a reference to the same girl being in three divorce cases. The investigation in this particular case resulted in one lawyer in Ontario being disbarred. Then we have this:
Few Divorces Rigged: Roberts
Attorney General Roberts says he is confident only a minority of Ontario divorce cases are rigged.
He told a McMaster University Progressive Conservative club meeting Monday night judges should not "let the wool be pulled over their eyes." Courts should be capable of deciding whether a divorce is rigged.
The question of whether divorce proceedings should be changed was a matter for federal, not provincial governments to decide.
Well, Mr. Speaker, we have sunk fairly low, I would think, when the attorney general would suggest to judges that they give more

Proposed Divorce Measures careful scrutiny to these cases; that some of them are faked, it is true, but the federal government is responsible for this and therefore we have not anything to do with it.
Divorce is not a nice thing. In my opinion divorce should be resorted to only as a last resort when married couples cannot get along. With all the opportunities that are afforded to married couples in our modern society, with marriage counsellors, with courts that are set up to give aid to those who are in trouble matrimonially, then divorce should only be a last resort. When divorce is resorted to I do not think it means we have to make our people lie and commit perjury, involve themselves in collusion and do all the other things we now ask them to do when they become involved with our federal divorce laws.
Divorces are going to be a part of our life whether we like it or not. We had a national rate of 35.7 per 100,000 in 1959, and it went as high as 65.6 per 100,000 of our population in 1947. Some of our provinces, British Columbia for instance, had a rate of 90.4 divorces per 100,000 of population, and Alberta had 67.3 per 100,000 of population. There was a total of 6,222 divorces in Canada in 1959. While we may not like divorce, Mr. Speaker, while we may see many things wrong with divorce, it is a fact that we have divorces. There is no longer any reason for people to hide their heads in the sand. I have dozens of letters indicating that there are people who are still hopeful the divorce laws will be changed in Canada so they can get married and legalize the unions to which they have had to resort because, in many cases, they did not have the money to go through the divorce procedures in the provinces in which they lived.
We have received hundreds of letters, and very few of them have been opposed to broadening the grounds upon which divorce is granted. While I would not go so far as to suggest that, in a political sense, this would be dishonest, I do suggest that it might not be politically sound. Surely a member of parliament does not have to listen to every crackpot in his particular riding. If we are going to be honest, then I think we will have to look facts in the face and give consideration to some of those facts.
I	am not hopeful that this bill will pass today. However, I am hopeful that a bill of this nature will pass in the very near future, because I have a great deal of confidence in the people. I would ask the members who sit in this house to be honest with themselves and with the country and do what they consider to be right in the light of all the facts. The election in Eastview renewed my faith

in the general public. I believe that in East-view the people learned the facts and made a decision, so democracy is still functioning.
Many hon. members believe that because they have certain religious organizations in their area, they should support these organizations. Members may find that these organizations do not express the opinion of the majority of the people in their ridings in this particular field. I have a letter here from Fillmore, Mullins, Gilhooly & Beairsto, barristers and solicitors in Kelowna, British Columbia. This is representative of many of the letters, many of the phone calls and many of the visits I have had from lawyers all across the country. The letter reads:
This is just a brief note to say that I think that the average person in this part of the country whether politically allied with you or (as in the case with me) not, approves of the blockade which you and other members of your party are conducting in the House of Commons against divorce bills. This may force some change in the impossible situation that has previously existed and it seems clear that nothing else could do so.
He sent a copy of this letter to his own federal member. In this regard I should like to tell the house that this year I have informed all those who have written to me that they could assist in this matter by writing to their member of parliament, and that they could also write to the Prime Minister recommending that now he have the courage and honesty to bring about a much better situation in connection with divorce in this country.
Now, many of the churches have written to me, Mr. Speaker, and I am quite sure most of them do not support my political party.
Mr. Pallet!: I wonder if the hon. member will explain what he meant by the expression that the Prime Minister should have honesty. That was a rather peculiar statement he made, and if there are any allusions to the Prime Minister's character I would ask the hon. member to withdraw immediately.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. What we were doing or what we intended to do was to show the transition between an action we took last year and what public opinion has requested in the introduction of this bill. While we intend to continue to fight as we did against the injustices that we considered were involved in the presentations in the house, the general public across Canada has indicated, as have lawyers, clergy and various others, that the solution not only rested in disposing of parliamentary divorce but that there was a great need in Canada for bringing up to date and modernizing the divorce law itself.
It may be unfortunate that under the British North America Act the matter of divorce was put under the jurisdiction of the federal government. It is a fact that in Canada there are many differences of opinion because of the geographical locations from which a Canadian may come. The conditions

Proposed Divorce Measures in the province of Newfoundland, on the one hand, may be much different from those in the province of British Columbia. Between those two extremes there are probably shades of opinion, one way or the other, concerning this matter across Canada. But the British North America Act gave to Canada the right to pass laws relating to the matter of marriage and divorce, and we have that responsibility. The provinces themselves can only accept the laws that we pass. Many of them at the present time, in my opinion, are aware of the failings and limitations of the act we now have, and are looking for something that is more in keeping with modern times.
This bill goes a little further than the bill that was introduced a short time ago in the United Kingdom. But as was said in the house here the other day, we are no longer a colony. We are not necessarily obliged to follow the British act as we did in the beginning. We have the right to do as we like in order to meet the needs of the Canadian people. This realization has resulted in the introduction of this bill.
In this bill we have tried to do two or three things that will provide remedies for all the people of Canada, no matter where they reside. One of the major problems was the fact that this law is still going to be administered, as probably should be the case, by the provinces themselves. We have left it with the provinces, so they can take up this bill and enact their own provincial laws to provide the divorce courts to administer this bill. This provision will mean that those provinces that want a liberal divorce law will be able to have one, and those that feel they cannot have any divorce law and do not want any divorce law can still exercise that right.
In the section that refers to domicile we have made a change that will allow relief even in those provinces that do not want divorce courts. We have made it so that those people coming from such a province will no longer be obliged to petition parliament but will be able to present their petition in a province other than the one in which they are normally resident. In order to do this we have changed, for divorce purposes only, the domicile clause that now applies.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the domicile clause was broadened in the divorce act of 1930, in the case of divorce, much more than is normally allowed by Canadian law. If passed, this bill would give the court jurisdiction to hear a divorce action if the parties were domiciled in any one of the ten provinces. For example, a wife in Quebec might 

petition in Ontario although her husband had changed his domicile to British Columbia. Normally if the husband had changed his domicile to British Columbia, in order to obtain a divorce the wife would have to follow his domicile and go to the province of British Columbia to seek a divorce. Now, because of the change in the divorce act of 1930, she can petition the parliament of Canada and retain the domicile of the province where she is normally domiciled.
This provision will broaden the act so that a wife having Canadian domicile will be able to apply for a divorce in any province of Canada, providing there is a divorce court set up in that province. It will also provide for cases where the husband has obtained domicile outside Canada since the marriage and the wife wishes to remain in Canada. Under this bill she may acquire a domicile of her own and the court may grant a divorce. This provision is wider than the legislation under the present Divorce Jurisdiction Act.
One of the major features of this bill that I think will be acceptable to all those who have examined it is the broadening of the grounds for divorce. We could refer to many, many newspaper articles, statements that have been made in the provincial courts, statements that have been made before the Senate and in the House of Commons before the miscellaneous private bills committee. It has been generally admitted that the ground upon which a divorce was being sought was adultery only because adultery was the only requisite, whereas really the divorce was being granted because of common law alliance, because of desertion or because the partner was in an institution for drug addiction, alcoholism or incurable insanity.
These various grounds have been provided in this bill. In each case, it should be brought to the attention of the house, the court will have power, under this bill, to exercise a great deal of jurisdiction in deciding whether or not these grounds are in the public interest. Therefore, though the grounds may be stated here, they are not recognized as grounds for divorce if the court can see some reason why the public interest would not be satisfied or met with these particular grounds.
As grounds for divorce we have provided adultery, desertion and cruelty. They are defined so as to repudiate or declare nonexistent the marriage relationship. We have provided for desertion in one form or another. For example, we have provided for voluntary desertion. We have provided for the granting of divorce on the ground of cruelty, either habitual or dangerous to the life of one of the parties. Clause 6 of the bill sets out a variety of grounds upon which the marriage

relationship could be dissolved; for example, perversion, habitual cruelty, and so on.
In each case where desertion is a ground for divorce we have put in a minimum of five years, so that desertion does not mean when somebody leaves for a week or two, as sometimes happens in the United States, where people leave for a very short period of time and come back and find they have been divorced on the ground of desertion. In each case the court is given the right under this bill to exercise its jurisdiction in relation to whether or not these things are for the good of Canada.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that in each of these grounds-and they are very extensive-we have taken into consideration both the public good and the requirements of the parties. I think we have made it possible for people to terminate their marriage through divorce without lying, without cheating, without involving themselves and their lawyers in collusion, without having to hire dishonest detectives, without having to incur undue, unnecessary expense.
We have tried to equalize opportunity in Canada as between the rich and the poor, so that it is no longer always possible for the rich to obtain a divorce while at the same time impossible for the poor to obtain one. We have, where possible, made it as easy for poor people to obtain justice as we have for rich people to obtain justice, bearing in mind at all times that it does not serve the country any good to have the lawyers, the judge, the court itself and all those connected with the divorce proceedings indulge in collusion and the other unpleasant things that we all know happen in divorce actions at the present time.
Mr. Speaker, in this bill we have not given consideration to a matter that we consider to be very important; that is the matter of the disposition of property and the custody of children. We are told-and the hon. senator who is chairman of the Senate divorce committee has made this statement on many occasions-that we already have the power, if we grant a divorce, to award custody of the children to either parent; we already have power to provide for the maintenance of those children. But in this bill, as soon as an action is taken, the province in which the divorce action is being heard will be able to grant the divorce; it will be able to grant custody of the children; it will be able to supervise maintenance and the operation of custody in the best manner, and serve the needs of the children in the best way. Therefore through this bill we have allowed the courts of the provinces to make this disposition of both property rights in alimony and the maintenance of children.

Proposed Divorce Measures
In this bill there is something I have recommended, as I know other members of this house have recommended it for a long time; that is, that we should not hear a divorce action until we have ascertained whether or not the parties can come together again. In this bill we have provided for the matter of reconciliation at the discretion of the court. The bill states:
9. It is the duty of the court in which a matrimonial cause has been instituted to give consideration, from time to time, to the possibility of a reconciliation of the parties to the marriage (unless the proceedings are of such a nature that it would not be appropriate to do so), and if at any time it appears to the judge constituting the court, either from the nature of the case, the evidence in the proceedings, or the attitude of those parties, or of either of them, or of counsel, that there is a reasonable possibility of such a reconciliation, the judge may do all or any of the following:
(a) adjourn the proceedings to afford those parties an opportunity of becoming reconciled or to enable anything to be done in accordance with either of the next two succeeding paragraphs;
This clause allows the judge himself, if he so wishes, to act as a judicial counsel to bring the parties together and hear the evidence. It also means that this judge will not again be able to hear that case, but that someone disinterested will hear the case if it is brought again before the court. It also means that any evidence given by the two parties in the matter of reconciliation, or any disclosure they may make, will be treated in secrecy and will never be allowed to appear in evidence.
Mr. Speaker, this is quite a broad change in our divorce act. I think all the clergy in Canada, irrespective of the denomination to which they belong, will be interested in studying these proposals. I have met many who have said they have not given any consideration to the changes which they would like to see brought about, and now they will have the opportunity of examining what can be done. They will, of course, give consideration to trying to keep married people together. It is our first and fundamental wish that those who are married should remain faithful to their marriage vows and live under them. Should this not be possible, however, we sincerely believe that in honour, and with the least inconvenience to the children of the marriage and to the nation, they should be able to obtain a divorce at a reasonable cost, in a reasonable manner and in a court which is capable of hearing all sides of the problem and reaching a decision, a decision from which there will be an opportunity to appeal.
I feel sure that if the government has any intention whatsoever of getting rid of the problem which we faced last session, and which we shall have to face in a much more

Proposed Divorce Measures severe form next year, it will be found to give consideration to changes such as are now being proposed, whether in this bill or in a similar bill. If the government wishes to put forward a bill of its own I shall be happy to withdraw the present bill in order to make it easier to do so.
I take no credit for introducing this measure. I did not get into this divorce business for my own satisfaction. I did so because I believe we have to do something about this question in Canada. I dislike the dishonesty which is now attached to our divorce proceedings, and in this I am sure I have the agreement of everyone in Canada who has given any consideration to this media of public opinion have been more than co-operative. Television and the other media of public opinion have been more than co-operative in this regard because they too believe we should not have a legal or jurisdictional settlement in this country which is based on hypocrisy, dishonesty and all the things which we hold should not figure in our judicial system.
Thus I would strongly urge the government to view this question as a whole and not to attack the individual parts of this bill. I will agree that the bill is not perfect. Indeed, one of my colleagues will move, when the bill reaches the committee stage, that we amend one of the clauses. No bill is perfect. Sometimes a minister of the crown, with all the assistance at his disposal, has to rise and ask that an amendment be made. We realize that amendments may have to be made to this bill, and the suggestions which hon. members may have to make may certainly be acceptable to me.
The important thing is that we should, this year and this session, get down to the business of enacting a more liberal minded divorce law in Canada.

speechtext:
In rising to take part in the debate on the bill now before the house, Bill No. C-2, I do not intend to go into the political implications or to discuss the morality or lack of morality of the divorce law, as did the hon. member who is sponsoring this measure. Nor do I intend to discuss the sufficiency or insufficiency of the evidence in the proceedings before parliament.
However, as the bill introduces an entirely new concept in divorce jurisdiction I want to confine myself entirely to the question of domicile as the basis for jurisdiction as far as Canadian divorce courts are concerned. The explanatory notes set out in the bill do not, in my opinion, set forth the whole purport of the bill. The bill provides that any court with the exception of courts in Newfoundland and Quebec shall have

jurisdiction to entertain a suit dealing with the marital relationship if the parties are domiciled in any one of the ten provinces.
This is an exceedingly wide departure from the present rule. We have no such thing as a national domicile or a Canadian domicile. A person has a domicile within the province in which the cause is being heard except under the special conditions prescribed by the Divorce Jurisdiction Act of 1930. As I indicated, I intend to discuss this bill primarily from the aspect of domicile rather than dealing with the enlargement of the grounds for divorce.
In order to understand the law of divorce in Canada and, certainly, the practice that exists in Canada, we must look back to the historical concept and the growth of divorce law and divorce procedure. We inherited most of our divorce law from the mother country and, to a large extent, our divorce practice also. The English courts, in turn, obtained most of their law from the Roman law and the canons of the Christian church. We find that through the years those canons of the Christian church and the Roman law have been modified to a considerable extent.
I have no quarrel with the basic fundamental concepts of the Roman law. I feel they have been a very stabilizing influence over the years; and although the Roman Catholic church does not, even today, grant an absolute divorce they have a judicial separation or, to use the judicial Latin phrase, a mensa et thoro, which is divorce from bed and board. But during the years and up to the time of Henry VIII-and this may be enlightenment to the sponsor of this bill- we find changes taking place, and a commission appointed by Henry VIII recommended that complete divorce should be granted on the grounds of adultery, desertion and cruelty.
It is also significant from a historical point of view that acts of divorce by parliament were of rare occurrence until the eighteenth century, when there were still only 134 divorces. In the first half of the nineteenth century there were 50. Apparently the procedure was so involved and so expensive that it was only available to the very rich. However, the average Englishmen felt there should be a relaxation of the divorce laws, and in 1845 Mr. Justice Maule, in sentencing a man for bigamy, used these words:
Prisoner at the bar: you have been convicted of the offence of bigamy, that is to say, of marrying a woman while you had a wife still alive, though it is true she hias deserted you and is living in adultery with another man. You have, therefore, committed a crime against the laws of your country, and you have also acted under a very serious misapprehension of the course which you ought to have pursued. You should have gone to the ecclesiastical court and there obtained against your wife a decree a mensa et thoro. You should then

have brought an action in the court of common law and recovered, as no doubt you would have recovered, damages against your wife's paramour. Armed with these decrees, you should have approached the legislature and obtained an act of parliament, which would have rendered you free and legally competent to marry the person whom you have taken on yourself to marry with no such sanction. It is quite true that these proceedings would have cost you many hundreds of pounds, whereas you probably have not as many pence. But the law knows no distinction between rich and poor. The sentence of the court upon you, therefore, is that you be imprisoned for one day, which period has already been exceeded, as you have been in custody since the commencement of the assizes.
I point that out to show that even in those days it was exceedingly difficult to obtain a divorce.
After the ecclesiastical courts gave up trying divorce actions the next development in England was the matrimonial causes act of 1857. This statute came into force on January 1, 1858, and created a court of record entitled "The Court for Divorce and Matrimonial Causes'', and it is from this statute of 1857 that the Canadian courts derive their jurisdiction.
When we examine the proposed bill we find that the jurisdiction is changed entirely. Under the English law, and under the law as administered by the courts of Canada, divorce can only be granted by the court of the person's domicile. A person at birth has what is known as a domicile of origin. That domicile of origin remains with him or her, in the case of a single person, until he or she acquires a domicile of choice. A domicile of choice can only be obtained by setting up or obtaining residence in a new country or in a new jurisdiction, with the intention of making your permanent home there. The English authorities and the Canadian authorities have not defined domicile with clarity. It has been defined by one judge as the centre of gravity, but it is usually interpreted as the place where a man or a person resides permanently and with the intention of remaining there permanently. If the domicile of choice is lost or abandoned, then the domicile of origin is retained.
The married woman, on the other hand, outside of the limited category in the Divorce Jurisdiction Act of 1930, has no separate domicile apart from her husband. Unless it is a case where she has been deserted for upwards of two years, she must bring the action where her husband is domiciled; but in the case of desertion for upwards of two years she may bring the action where her husband was domiciled at the time of the desertion.
The present bill not only provides for a Canadian domicile-that is, a person domiciled in the province of New Brunswick is
Proposed Divorce Measures domiciled in every other province of Canada for the purpose-but enables a married woman to acquire a domicile separate and apart from her husband; and if I read section 4 subsection 2 correctly, it provides that a married woman may petition the court where she is residing, providing her husband was domiciled in any province of Canada at the time of the marriage, and so obtain a divorce provided, of course, the other requirements for divorce are present. At least she sets up that the court has jurisdiction.
Hon. members will realize, I think, that this is a very wide extension of the present law and of the jurisdiction of the court. Canadian divorces, as they are now granted on the basis of domicile, are recognized throughout the world, and I think this is as it should be. Any divorce-and I am talking now of absolute divorce, not judicial separation-makes a change in the status of the individuals concerned. It is more than an action in persona; it is an action in rem. It affects the status of the people; it affects property rights; in nullity actions it affects the legitimacy or illegitimacy of the children, and I submit that we should not so widen the basis of jurisdiction as to allow any weakening of the position of the Canadian courts, or allow decrees to be granted on any basis except the basis of domicile.
In recent years in some of our courts there has been a tendency in nullity actions, especially actions that are void, to be satisfied on the basis of residence, or at least it would appear that the evidence establishes residence more than domicile. But I submit that the weakness of the present bill is twofold. One, it is trying to set up a national domicile. Now, an individual can have only one domicile at one time. Domicile is peculiar, particular to a certain geographical and legal entity. That should remain as it is. The second weakness is that a married woman who is separated from her husband can acquire a national or a provincial domicile regardless of the present whereabouts of her husband, or whether he has acquired a new domicile beyond the domicile he had at the time of the marriage.
I point these things out to indicate that the English and the Canadian basis of jurisdiction, namely that of domicile, is much more satisfactory and provides an adequate assurance that any petitioner coming before the courts, if he establishes domicile and has the necessary evidence, will obtain a divorce, or a divorce can be obtained.
I intimated that I was not going to discuss the grounds as set out in the proposed bill. I think most of us are agreed that there should be an extension of some of the grounds.

Proposed Divorce Measures but I cannot support *wholeheartedly the grounds set out in the bill. I think they would have a tendency to make divorces too easy to obtain; that, coupled with the question of domicile, they would leave the way open for abuses, for collusion and connivance, and would defeat one of the purposes of the sponsors of this bill. It is submitted that domicile should be the basis of divorce actions and should also be the basis of nullity actions, and if those actions were brought in the various provincial courts I think many of the objections to the present proceedings in parliament would be abolished.
We cannot force on any provincial government an act compelling them to set up a divorce court. That is a matter entirely within the provincial realm. It is true that under the British North America Act divorce is assigned to the federal government, but I submit to the house that at the present time all the provincial courts, I think without exception, are operating under preconfederation statutes. We obtain our divorce jurisdiction based on domicile from the imperial parliament.

subtopic: MEASURE TO MODERNIZE DISSOLUTION AND ANNULMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house is now considering a bill which might have some very serious effects, as it involves first the whole matrimonial institution, then the constitution, at least as far as the province of Quebec is concerned, and also in a general way, the entire social order which, by tradition, has rested on the family.
I wish I could have had a little more time to study all the aspects of the divorce problem, but even at the risk of missing certain points, I think in the face of this measure, I should immediately state my position on the principles involved.
First, let me comment briefly on the bill itself. It is a bill on divorce in Canada, and its obvious purpose is to facilitate and generalize divorce in this country. For any person domiciled in Canada, this bill in effect proposes that the administration of the act be a responsibility of the courts; clause 4 of the bill is quite definite on that point. It gives the courts the power to hear divorce cases between spouses domiciled in any one of the ten provinces of Canada. Indeed, the explanatory notes on this clause read as follows:
Thus, for example, a wife in Quebec may petition in Ontario although her husband has changed his domicile to British Columbia.
[Mr. Stewart.}

Now if we look at the grounds for divorce listed in clause 6 or at the grounds for annulment of marriage in clause 8, we find with some astonishment that thousands of marriages could be broken up under such grounds.
While respecting the views of the mover of this bill, and of those hon. members who feel they should agree with him, I honestly believe that, if such legislation were passed, we would have in our statutes an act that would shake up our whole social order, one that would strike at the very roots of marriage and of family life, which we have always considered to be the cornerstone of our society.
American experience in this field proves that divorce courts invariably apply the divorce laws liberally, not restrictively, as in the case of civil law or criminal law, with the practical result that such legislation indirectly leads to free cohabitation. I think that, in the face of such consequences, we should not hesitate a single moment, and not only vote against this bill, but condemn the state of mind which inspired it.
Having said that, I want to go a little further and delve more deeply into the problem of divorce from our point of view as members of parliament. Let us not delude ourselves, for we are facing serious difficulty, and no matter how we look at it, the solution is not easy.
What happened in this house during the last session, when divorce bills were under scrutiny, certainly did not heighten prestige of parliament in the eyes of the public. Members will recall that, last year, several hundred divorce bills were deliberately blocked during most of the session and were then all passed at once in the last days of the session. The government did not dare to take a definite position at that time, but I feel that time for a solution is running short.
Last year-I am speaking from memory- probably more than 600 divorce bills were brought before us from Quebec and Newfoundland. There may be even more this year, and in two years from now we may get them by the thousand. When that number is reached, will the upper house be compelled to make consideration of divorce bills a full time job for all hon. senators?
As we can all realize, those bills are a nuisance to the Senate, to the government and to the members of this house. The divorce

problem simultaneously involves constitutional, parliamentary and religious aspects. However, that is not a reason for dealing with it in a timorous way. I believe that, in discussing the bill, we should assume our responsibilities and I shall briefly outline the background of the matter from that angle-at least with regard to the province of Quebec- before making a suggestion which, I believe, might serve as a basis for the settlement of this problem.
Before Canada was ceded in 1760, the customary law of Paris where legislation was based on French and Catholic principles, proclaimed that marriage could not be dissolved, and did not tolerate divorce in the territory which was to become Lower Canada, and later still, the province of Quebec. That legislation which remains the basis of civil law in the province of Quebec, only accepted separation.
Our civil law remained fully the same following the cession of 1760, and later on our practices and customs in civil law, that is French law, of which indissolubility of wedlock was a part, were confirmed by the Quebec Act of 1774.
In 1865, the joint parliament of the two Canadas adopted for Lower Canada the same, though newly codified civil code which, under section 185, provided the indissolubility of marriage in exactly the same terms that are to be found today in our code, that is the following:
-marriage can only be dissolved by the natural demise of one of the partners. As long as they both live, it is indissoluble.
Then came the British North America Act in 1867. It was at that time, I think, that, according to the various authors I read, the problem came up which seems so complicated to us today.
Before they joined confederation, the provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, as well as British Columbia had their own divorce laws. In fact, a provision in the British North America Act- under section 129, I think-stipulated that provinces which had their own divorce laws before joining confederation would keep them as they were.
Following a decision by the privy council in 1919-in the case of Board v. Board, as reported in volume A.C., page 956-the prairie provinces obtained that right with regard to divorce. Since then, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta have their own divorce courts.
Proposed Divorce Measures
It was during the session of 1930 that, under the Woodsworth's bill, it was decided that a divorce court would be established in Ontario. Incidentally, we may note-and this is quite interesting-that the main argument advanced by Mr. Woodsworth, then leader of the C.C.F. party, was that the number of divorce cases was constantly on the rise and that they were becoming an embarrassment for parliament; now, according to him, an Ontario divorce court would have the effect of reducing that number. Events have proved him wrong.
On the other hand, subsection 13 of section 92 of the B.N.A. Act confers to provinces the exclusive right of legislating on civil rights, and it can be said-as various distinguished lawyers actually did say-that with regard to Quebec, the constitution of 1867 confirmed the provisions of our civil code, including section 185 which proclaims the indissolubility of marriage.
I shall now come back to the B.N.A. Act. Section 91 of that act endows the federal government with jurisdiction in respect of anything affecting marriage and divorce, except the actual celebration of marriage.
From that viewpoint, one must come to the conclusion, as far as Quebec is concerned, that the constitution provides for double jurisdiction. This, to my mind, is the crux of the problem.
To back this up, I should like to quote what a former prime minister of Canada, the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent had to say in that connection on March 24, 1944, as reported in a book entitled Le probleme du divorce, by Rev. Father de Lery.
Not only has Quebec no jurisdiction in divorce matters, but there is a statute dating back to before the confederation, maintained in force through the B.N.A. Act and which will remain in force as long as parliament does not decide to legislate in the matter, as authorized under section 91 of the constitution. That statute, which was in force at the time of confederation, provides that marriage shall be dissolved only by death of the husband or the wife. No matter what authority is set up, so long as that legislation is in force in the province, no divorce may be granted by any court.
The solution to the problem therefore appears a little more clearly now. Eight provinces now have divorce courts and, therefore, for the moment, there is no problem there as far as the federal government is concerned. The matter is entirely different in the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland where no divorce courts are in existence and divorce was never recognized.
Before joining confederation, Newfoundland had not granted a single divorce. The province of Quebec has always opposed

Proposed Divorce Measures divorce. In short, neither province wants a divorce court. Therefore, I should like to ask the following question: Why not respect the wishes of those two provinces? Has it occurred to us that by granting to the people of those two provinces, Quebec and Newfoundland, the right to divorce, we would be imposing upon them rights and privileges which they are not seeking? Now, how can we reconcile the federal government's constitutional right to grant divorce with the civil law of both those provinces, which do not recognize divorce and have no wish to do so?
It has been contended by certain people that divorce cases might be referred to the Exchequer Court of Canada. It would be interesting, I think, to read what the author quoted previously, Rev. de Lery has to say about this in his book Le problems du divorce, page 104:
In the face of obvious opposition to the suggestion of giving Quebec and Newfoundland courts jurisdiction in divorce matters, it has been suggested that authority in the matter be devolved upon the exchequer court or some other federal court.
If divorce cases are referred to any court, provincial or federal, on either shore of the Ottawa river, any person in Newfoundland and Quebec would obtain an undeniable right to petition that court, for when a court is in existence, any citizen has a right to apply to it for redress of any damage sustained. And that court would have to grant or refuse the divorce on the sole basis of the law and the evidence. The granting of a divorce was formerly an act of grace, a favour; it would now become a matter of strict right. To set up a court is to recognize divorce. This is more than a matter of convenience of procedure. There is a principle involved.
I think we should put an end to this paradoxical, indeed slightly ridiculous situation, by leaving to the provinces full and exclusive jurisdiction in the field of marriage.
Let the provinces themselves decide whether they want divorce courts, and in the affirmative, let them determine when and how they may from time to time, if they so wish, extend the grounds for divorce.
If the government amended section 71-* this is a suggestion-to remove from the federal parliament jurisdiction over marriage and divorce, the provinces would then exercise full and exclusive jurisdiction in this field. Such a course would not only eliminate a source of considerable annoyance for parliament, which can only increase over the years, but it would also return to the provinces a jurisdiction which is intimately tied' up with the exercise of their civil rights. I have always felt, and those who have had to deal with constitutional problems have always felt, that there is nothing more local and more provincial than marriage ties.


So the sooner we can hand over this field to the provinces, the better it will be for everyone.
