subtopic: MEASURE TO MODERNIZE DISSOLUTION AND ANNULMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to follow the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stewart) and the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) and to have had the opportunity to listen to the ideas they put forward in reference to this bill with regard to divorce. In listening to their arguments I was almost convinced that many times, on many problems in Canada, we are divided not so much by political parties as by regions, environment and experiences.
On this occasion I should like to congratulate the mover of the bill. I think I can say that I am with him in spirit. There are some things about the bill with which, as I develop my argument this afternoon, I will take issue. However, I know that in presenting the bill he felt there were certain changes that should be made with reference to the divorce law of Canada. I could not go along with him in the idea that because some people in Canada had written to him and expressed views different from his own, whether they look at the matter from the ecclesiastical point of view or otherwise, they are crackpots. The reason I am a Conservative is because I am happy that we have a leader like the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) who spelled out the rights that we have as Canadians. One of those rights is the right to worship as we see fit. In dealing with this particular matter we cannot isolate that consideration entirely.
I am also happy to take part in the debate today because, coming as I do from the city of Calgary and speaking as a westerner, I should like to make reference to a gentleman who is a great scholar, namely Mr. W. Kent Power, Q.C., a distinguished constitutional lawyer and a great gentleman who for many years has expressed his viewpoint on this subject. I know you will not mind my digressing for a moment, Mr. Speaker, in order to make reference to this gentleman who has shown in many ways the needs in reference to this matter and who has also written many textbooks with reference to the divorce law of Canada. He is also, as I said, a distinguished constitutional lawyer. For a number of years I have been indirectly associated with him and I know that in this field he is a real reformer and that he conscientiously believes that certain changes should be made. He has so expressed himself

in various organizations, particularly the Canadian Bar Association, from time to time.
In the beginning I might say that it is not easy for any member of parliament to rise in his place and speak on this matter of divorce. Every member of parliament must appreciate the fact that in the area from which he comes there are people who have different views on the subject. It is therefore not an easy subject to discuss. I do not know just how one should look at the matter but I am convinced the law must be changed. If there is any law of Canada that allows the dissolution of marriage, that law should ensure to the individual certain rights, dignity, compassion and justice. From listening to the various hon. members express their views today I feel that the law as it stands today in Canada is inadequate and archaic. It is my opinion-and I am going to repeat it-that if we are to have a divorce law at all in Canada it should serve the individual with dignity, compassion and justice.
This is not a new subject here, Mr. Speaker. This is not a new subject for civilization. It is not a new subject for Canada. It is not a new subject for any country. We can go back into some of the oldest records. In fact, we can go back-and I say this with the greatest of respect-to the Bible itself. I am now quoting from chapter 24 of Deuteronomy wherein is found expressed at that time the very problem we are now debating in our civilization today. In quoting from chapter 24 I am just going to read two or three verses. I make this reference only in order to show that it is not a new problem in society. From the beginning of society some men and women who have lived together for the purpose of producing a family have had problems. The foundation of every civilization is the family. I read from chapter 24 of Deuteronomy as follows:
When a man hath taken a wife, and married her, and it come to pass that she find no favour in his eyes, because he hath found some uncleanness in her: then let him write her a bill of divorcement, and give it in her hand, and send her out of his house.
2.	And when she is departed out of his house, she may go and be another man's wife.
3.	And if the latter husband hate her, and write her a bill of divorcement, and giveth it in her hand, and sendeth her out of his house; or if the latter husband die, which took her to be his wife;
4.	Her former husband, which sent her away, may not take her again to be his wife, after that she is defiled; for that is abomination before the Lord: and thou shalt not cause the land to sin, which the Lord thy God giveth thee for an inheritance.
5.	When a man hath taken a new wife, he shall not go out to war, neither shall he be charged with any business: but he shall be free at home one year, and shall cheer up his wife which he hath taken.
Proposed Divorce Measures
I refer to that quotation with the greatest respect in order to show that this is not a new problem.
Today we have had various references to the question of jurisdiction, particularly by the hon. member for Charlotte. I am going to refer for a few moments to this distinguished author who lives in Calgary and who today is retired from the active practice of law, and to what he has to say about jurisdiction. In doing so I may say that I am now speaking from a western viewpoint; I am speaking as a westerner from western Canada. I would be loath to speak on the subject, as far as the law is concerned, in reference to any of the other provinces than the prairie provinces because in various provinces the laws are different. When one makes a statement as to what appears to be the law in other regions on this subject or any other subject he must be careful.
The book from which I intend to quote is entitled "The Law of Divorce in Canada" by W. Kent Power, 1948. Of course, he has brought it up to date from time to time. In the paragraph of the said book at page 1 he states as follows:
Only the dominion parliament can legislate in relation to the substantive law of divorce. Exclusive jurisdiction over the subject was assigned to parliament by the British North America Act, 1867, sec. 91 (26)-"Marriage and divorce." Therefore, no provincial legislature or delegate thereof can enact a divorce law where, as in Quebec, none exists, or interfere with the substantive provisions of the law now in force, whether by a superseding act or by altering, adding to, suspending or repealing it. The word "divorce" in sec. 91 has not been judicially defined. Since, however, the B.N.A. Act of 1867 was passed by the imperial parliament after its enactment of the Divorce and Matrimonial Causes Act of 1857 in which "divorce" means the dissolution of a marriage-
I might pause there, Mr. Speaker, to say this. We in Alberta and Saskatchewan, of which I think I have some knowledge, have the same identical law as that which existed in Great Britain in 1857. That is the law that prevailed because of the British North America Act; I refer to the substantive law. Of course provincial statutes can make the law in reference to procedure and as to how we can proceed with a divorce action when it comes before the courts in question. Therefore, from my point of view, with regard to the area from which I come I think it can be safely said that this particular parliament has the jurisdiction with which to change the divorce law of this country.
In reference to jurisdiction, of course, we have the question of domicile, and the hon. member for Charlotte mentioned this matter. The definition of domicile is defined as follows: "The place where a person does reside and intends to make his permanent residence, or where he was born, which is that
624	HOUSE OF
Proposed Divorce Measures person's domicile of origin." Unfortunately, it has always been the domicile of the husband that has governed the jurisdiction of the court. In that regard, in implementing the law as it stands, it has worked-as one hon. member said-some hardship on the people seeking remedy in that regard.
Then, of course, we have the Divorce Jurisdiction Act which has somewhat remedied the situation. That act gives the right to bring an action in that province where a person is residing, providing two years have lapsed since the desertion in that province where the husband was domiciled at the time the desertion took place.
That seems to cover the question of domicile fairly thoroughly as far as the Alberta and Saskatchewan courts are concerned. However, when you look at the grounds for divorce I suppose it depends, when you are discussing it, whether one looks at the marriage relationship from a spiritual or a contractual point of view. I was rather interested, Mr. Speaker, at the reference today to the book written in a rather satirical manner by A. P. Herbert, a former member of parliament in Great Britain. At the time he was working for the reform of British divorce laws, which were eventually changed in 1937 and have been changed somewhat since then. He deals with this matter strictly on a contract basis. As I said, it depends on the way you look at it. I will quote from his book "Holy Deadlock". Those who have not read the book would find it most interesting, even if they do not agree with it, because it is written in a very humorous fashion and illustrates how divorces were obtained in England before the time of the reform of their divorce laws. On page 16 of the Penguin series book he has this to say:
A man might jeopardize the lives of soldiers by his orders, the safety of the state by his vote, the property of his employers by his arithmetic, his own welfare by his choice of a partner or profession; but all such errors were forgotten, or could, at least, be corrected, by a man of character. Only in the most difficult choice of all- the choice of a partner, not for business, but for life-was a young man expected to be infallible, considered caddish if he confessed to error, and treated as a criminal if he attempted to correct it.
Very odd. And yet the wise and pious state took no trouble at all to prevent the young man from making the mistake, to impose delay between the decision and the fatal step. A decree of divorce was not made absolute until six months after the wise judge had decided that there ought to be a divorce-for fear the wise judge might have made a mistake. But there was no decree nisi for marriage: the foolish young man could tie himself up for life seven days after he had made his decision by walking into a register office and filling up a form or two. Very odd. All those laws and regulations to prevent a man from eating the wrong things, drinking the wrong things, seeing
[Mr. Woolliams.j

the wrong pictures, reading the wrong books, working in the wrong way-but nothing at all to prevent a man from marrying the wrong wife. But what a fuss if he admitted his mistake and wanted to marry the right one!
It depends how you look at it. If you look at it from a contractual point of view, that expressed the situation well. But as I said at the outset-and I repeat it now-it just depends how you look at it. If you look at it from the spiritual point of view, I come back to the bill of rights, that every Canadian has the right to make the decision according to his conscience. Some are for changes in the divorce law; some are against any change; but all people in Canada who express themselves in whatever manner they wish do it certainly with the proper conscience.
Let us look at what the law is today in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, which have similar divorce laws. A divorce action is brought in the superior court of Saskatchewan, in the Queen's bench division; in Alberta it is brought in the supreme court trial division. What must be proved? First of all the party applying for the divorce issues a statement of claim in the court having jurisdiction. In some provinces this is done by a petition. They must prove domicile. I have already given the definition of domicile and I will not repeat it.
Then the marriage itself must be proved, and this is generally done by a marriage certificate. Then the parties must prove they have cohabited; in other words they have lived together as man and wife. Then-and I will have something to say about this later-the adultery must be proved. Then they must negative the questions of collusion and connivance. All of the facts are set out in a statement of claim, and when there is no statement of defence filed under the rules of court with jurisdiction after a certain period the action is set down for trial before a court with jurisdiction as an undefended action. There is a difference between the procedure in various provinces. The substantive law I maintain can be changed by this parliament and the power to do so rests with the federal government.
However, the rules governing the procedure are controlled by the provinces. In the province of Alberta-I do not say this in any critical way-it is much easier to obtain a divorce than it is in the province of Saskatchewan. This is because in the province of Saskatchewan they adopted a procedure which is very cumbersome. You have to file an affidavit of bona fides. The affidavit has to prove all the five points I have mentioned and of course has to negative collusion and connivance. After you have filed the affidavit,

a statement of claim is filed. Even if the action is undefended, you have to serve the statement of claim on all parties, the corespondent and the defendant. In the Saskatchewan courts I have seen cases where one mistake in procedure would cause the action to be dismissed and one would have to start all over again.
But this is not true in the province of Alberta, because over the years in Alberta the governments, or those who have power to prepare the rules of court, have streamlined the procedure. You merely file a statement of claim, and if after 15 days-and you reside in that province-no defence has been filed in the court the action is noted in default for a statement of defence and it can be preciped down for trial.
If someone is defending the action on the question of custody of the children, or some other defence, he files a demand of notice and the action can be heard within ten or 15 days. They have streamlined the procedure. In one province it is difficult; in the other province it is not so difficult.
So there is some onus on provincial governments to change the procedure if they feel it is cumbersome and should be speeded up. Of course, that rests entirely on the governments of the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta. I need not say any more in that regard.
I want to say something now about proof of adultery. It has not been suggested since I have been a member of parliament, nor have I read anywhere, that divorce laws should be repealed. If we accept that there should be divorce laws, let us make these laws such that they will serve the individual with dignity, compassion and justice.
In proving adultery, on many occasions we have to-as it has been called-put our dirty linen on the line. In many cases this is very embarrassing. More than that, I am convinced, with the experience I have had in reference to these matters in my profession, that on many, many occasions the marriage has failed long before there is any proof or suggestion of adultery. I will come to that matter in reference to proof of adultery.
As one great jurist said, "It is very seldom adultery is committed in threes". Therefore the judge must presume certain facts, certain situations and circumstances. As one great writer pointed out-and I must say that we have never had this problem in Alberta-if the evidence is that there is only one occasion on which adultery was committed the judge may presume it was so seldom that it likely did not happen. But if there were too many occasions, he might think they had stretched the truth and presumed against the parties. The action would be dismissed in each case.
Proposed Divorce Measures
This matter is generally proved on the question of presumption. I say now, standing in my place, that my experience in the two provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta is that we have the highest calibre of men on the bench in these provinces. I want to answer some criticism that has been made from time to time from a certain part of this house in connection with collusion and perjury in divorce actions and cases. Perjury itself does not only occur in divorce cases. Witnesses have been found guilty of committing perjury when dealing with a question of land dispute or erecting fences.
Let me say that I am convinced that in the majority of cases that come before the courts of Alberta and Saskatchewan there is no collusion. We read about collusion in newspapers and they tend to exaggerate those exceptional cases where there has been perjury or something cooked up.
A great many people have the idea-and I listened to the letter read by the hon. member today-that if the parties do see each other that might be collusion. I do not think that is the law. I want to read from Mr. Kent Power's book "The Law of Divorce in Canada" page 65, and this is what the court of appeal of Manitoba has said, and I believe it has been accepted by the courts of appeal of Alberta and other provinces:
In order to constitute collusion there must be a corrupt agreement or conspiracy-
Let us deal with that for a moment. It must be that the parties sit down together, and George says: I am going out today to do the very thing necessary for you to get a divorce. That would be to conspire to do a wrongful act. But the fact that husband says: "Good morning, Helen" or the wife says "Hello, George" or they discuss the question of the custody of the children, or how much maintenance should be paid is certainly not collusion. That is where many writers and newspapers have been led down the wrong path and led astray. Now let us go on with the definition:
-to which the petitioner is a party, to obtain a divorce by manufactured evidence-
Manufactured evidence is evidence which has been cooked up or planned, or somebody goes on the stand to commit perjury or practices deceit on the court. When we talk about collusion, in 90 per cent of the cases that, to me, is a falsehood. To state that in the percentage of cases there is collusion is a slight on the judiciary of Canada. I am confident, and I repeat, the judges of Alberta and the judges I have been before in Saskatchewan were able to determine in a judicious matter what people were telling the truth and what people were not. That does not mean they would not make an
626	HOUSE OF
Proposed Divorce Measures error, but it suggests to me that 90 per cent or more of the cases that go before the courts are justifiable cases, and the six facts I have mentioned are properly proved, for example, domicile, the marriage and cohabitation; that there was no collusion, no connivance. That has been my experience and, I am going to repeat, those newspaper articles which say all these cases are collusive are overstating the case for the purpose of getting a change in the law, and that is not good enough. There must be other substantial arguments.
It is interesting to see what Herbert had to say in reference to one other fact before I leave the question of proof. One strange fact, and I think this is one argument in favour of extending the law to other grounds than adultery, is that if the plaintiff spouse is guilty of adultery there is an onus on the solicitor for the plaintiff to lay those facts before the court. I say I am confident that in 99.9 per cent of the cases the lawyers, who are officers of the court, do lay those offences before the courts. If both parties are guilty of adultery the case could be dismissed because the judge can exercise his discretion against the plaintiff, which does seem rather strange, where both are guilty. If both parties are guilty of adultery, then it may be against public policy to grant the divorce. It is a matter of discretion based on the old Roman law and ecclesiastical law. That again is proof that over the years our courts have been able to exercise equity with a great deal of dignity. This is what Herbert has to say about this subject on page 81:
This was always a difficult matter, the framing of the safety question. A solicitor is an officer of the court. It is his duty to disclose to the court the fact that a petitioner for divorce has herself been guilty of adultery, if he is aware of it. It is his duty to his client to warn her that if she has committed adultery she must disclose it; for otherwise she may wander innocently into trouble with the King's proctor.
Now I am just going to pause there. In every province they have a Queen's proctor, or the job is done by the attorney general, and between the time of the order nisi and the final order the case can be reviewed if there is a complaint and then they can file notice of intervention and have a trial on that subject, and I have seen it happen in many cases. I continue:
The conscientious solicitor, therefore, satisfies himself before he begins. That is to say, he puts to his clients questions the answers to which may 'tend to show that she has been guilty of adultery.' Such questions may not be put to her in court by counsel or judge, and need not be answered, unless she has already given evidence to the contrary effect.
I must say, from my experience of the Alberta and Saskatchewan law societies that where a lawyer has had brought to his


attention by his client that there is adultery on both sides he immediately lays those facts before the trial judge. He puts his faith in those men who have been elevated to that high position to grant justice if it is a deserving case and, in my experience in that regard, justice is always done.
Now, with reference to what changes should be made, let us have a look at that for a few moments. This bill, I feel, goes a little further than it should, and I have not time to go into it, but it does seem to me that where there is incurable insanity that should be a ground; where there has been desertion for a period of three or five years, whatever a committee might consider best, that should be a ground; and also where someone has been confined to life imprisonment. I know a case where a person got 20 years within a few days of his marriage. That should be a ground.
But however far the grounds are extended, as they were extended in 1937 in Great Britain, one thing I believe, because I believe that the home is the foundation of society, is that there should be retained in that act certain safeguards. Maybe no one should have the right to make any application until he or she has been married for three or five years or longer. That would put the necessary caution into the minds of people before they enter into the marriage in question, and I believe that in some respects this has been spelled out by the British act in 1937. But, and I repeat, desertion should, of course, be a question of whether a person has been deserted for three years.
When I say those changes should be made, I base my argument not on the fact that I get letters pro and con but on what I see in society about me. Truly we do not know how many thousands of people are living in Canada today who, one spouse or the other, went across to the United States and got a form of divorce which is not legal in this country because the husband was not properly domiciled in this country. Those people then returned to their own land and they are subject to the Criminal Code to be charged with bigamy. It was my experience to defend one of these people in that regard.
There are, as Mr. Kent Power has said, thousands of people living in Canada in bigamous circumstances, and that is not all- what about the children, where do they stand? Are they legitimate or illegitimate? What about the marital status of the parties. What about property reports? Many times there is the question whether it is the first wife or the after-taken wife, inherits the property when a husband dies? This is quite a mess as far as the administration of these estates are concerned and the security of the

family is concerned. So I say on those facts, and because the facts to prove adultery in many cases occur after the marriage has fallen apart, there should be an enlargement of the grounds for divorce, and I base that on the premise that if we are to have any divorce law in Canada at all we should make it a law which is reasonable and which can be applied with dignity and justice. I think I have made my point clear in that regard.
The bill has gone somewhat farther but, to be fair, I must say that it is a step in the right direction, because it brings to the attention of the people of Canada a very important matter which has been under consideration for many years. It is a problem that will not be solved easily. We must have patience. It is a matter that we must always consider with great tact because in this country of many races and religions people have different ideas. All of those ideas in this great country of ours must be respected, because never should we allow the minority to be coerced by the majority or vice versa. Therefore, I feel this is a matter which should be considered and debated carefully. This is why I listened with great interest to one of the members from French Quebec who expressed his views based on provincial rights and provincial jurisdiction. That is why I say once again this matter must be considered carefully. Every member of parliament represents people of various races and religions. We are the spokesmen of those people, the hired men, as it were, who were sent here to express their point of view.
In a sincere way I have tried, Mr. Speaker, to bring this problem forcibly before the House of Commons as I see it, but with the greatest respect for all those who share other ideas, knowing full well that the problem will not be solved overnight.

subtopic: MEASURE TO MODERNIZE DISSOLUTION AND ANNULMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are now considering an extremely delicate problem, one that should be handled carefully. At the outset of my remarks, may I say that throughout my speech, I intend to respect the views of those who disagree with me. Indeed, as was mentioned by the previous speaker, there are so many different views in relation to the provinces and to the religious aspects, that we should respect the religious feelings of all members of the house. That is what I propose to do in the course of my remarks.
When the Senate was asked to broaden the divorce act to make divorces easier to get, I decided to study the matter more thoroughly
Proposed Divorce Measures in case it might come up before the house. I wanted to explain my opposition to such a move, not only as a Catholic, but as a believer in God, the Creator and ultimate end of man.
For those who believe in and accept the Bible-both the Old and the New Testament-as inspired books expressing the will of the Creator, that is where the answer to the problem can be found. The first reference to marriage, even though that term is not used, is in Genesis, where God says:
It is not good that man should be alone; I will make him an helpmeet lor him.
This is in Genesis, 2-18.
Then God proceeded to create woman, and it is said that the first words spoken by Adam were divinely inspired and were willed by the Creator. I quote:
This is now hone of my bones, and flesh ol my flesh.
He called her woman because she was taken out of man. This may be found in the Book of Genesis 2-23.
As we can see, according to the divine plan, marriage was intended to be and was the very close union between two human beings, male and female, of equal dignity, such union being inseparable.
In view of that statement, some people will be inclined to wonder why then, so soon after the creation, men started to take many wives, make them their slaves, and even sell them as if they were so many chattels? The answer is that the plan of God was soon put aside by people, and let no one make the disastrous mistake of confusing the laws of God and the actions of mankind. Nowhere will you find a shadow of divine approbation for those human actions, even in the case of those who seemed to enjoy a greater intimacy with God, like Abraham.
It is also true that in Mosaic law, there is a divorce provision; however, it was not introduced with the divine approval, but as a hypothetical case. We find the explanation in the New Testament, which is a clarification of the Old Testament, when Our Lord answered to the Pharisees who, to tempt Him, had asked:
Is it lawful for a man to put away his wife?
And Jesus replied:
Have you not read that from the beginning the Creator made them man and wife and that He said: "For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and cleave to his wife; And they twain shall be one flesh: so then they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder." And they (the Pharisees) said:	"Moses suffered to

Proposed Divorce Measures write a bill of divorcement, and to put her away. And Jesus answered and said unto them, For the hardness of your heart he wrote you this precept." But at the beginning it was not so.
Is this not a condemnation of divorce? But to properly understand Moses, we must recognize that the Jews were a nomadic people, whose intellectual development was very limited, and whom the Egyptians had kept in bondage for hundreds of years. We must therefore understand that Yahweh tolerated things which he never approved. Besides you will find in the prophets many a condemnation of the practice of divorce. In Matthew, Luke or Paul, we always find the absolute, never exceptions.
Here is an example of what St. Luke says (16-18):
Whosoever putteth away his wife, and marrieth another, committeth adultery: and whosoever marrieth her that is put away from her husband committeth adultery.
Now St. Paul in his Epistle to the Romans (7;2-3) said:
For the woman which hath an husband is bound by the law to her husband so long as he liveth; but if the husband be dead, she is loosed from the law of her husband. So then, if, while her husband liveth, she be married to another man, she shall be called an adulteress',-
That quotation might lead people to think that divorce is only forbidden to women; but, if we go back to Genesis (2;24) where it is said:
"And they shall be one flesh,"
We realize that it clearly applies to both- man and woman. However, St. Paul was much more precise when writing to the Corinthians (1-7; 10-11):
And unto the married I command, yet not I, but the Lord:	Let not the wife depart from her
husband. But, and if, she depart, let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her husband; and let not the husband put away his wife.
As you may see, this is absolute, and I believe that on a matter of such importance, if there had been a possible exception, either St. Paul or St. Luke, or St. Matthew, would have mentioned it, because they were the spokesmen of Christ, and we cannot accuse them of misrepresentation. Therefore, the prohibition of divorce with the right to remarry, is absolute.
Some of those who are in favour of divorce think they have found a contradiction in St. Matthew (19:9) where it is reported that Christ told the Pharisees:
And I say unto you, whosoever shall put away his wife, except it be for lewdness-
-or fornication according to some translators-
-and shall marry another, committeth adultery. 

The words: "except it be for lewdness" (or fornication, according to some translators) seem to allow for an exception. However, we should not forget that we are dealing with a translation from the Greek, and that is why some translate the word porneia by "lewdness" and others by "fornication". Which word should we choose? Most English versions translate porneia by "fornication" and, if we take the definitions of various dictionaries, I would opine that the word "fornication" was the one Our Lord wanted to use.
What does Larousse say with regard to lewdness?:
Unchaste character-The lewdness of prostitutes.
As it may well be that a married woman be a prostitute, there would be a contradiction if Christ had said that a prostitute may be repudiated.
Here is how the Larousse dictionary defines "fornication":
Fornication: A simple sin of the flesh, that is to say sexual intercourse between persons that are neither married nor bound by a vow.
And in "The New Catholic Dictionary", Vatican Edition 1929, the definition is as follows:
(Text):
Fornication: The free act of carnal intercourse between persons who are not married, but who are free to marry.
(Translation):
With those definitions in mind, the word fornication seems to me to translate the Greek word porneia.
Furthermore, the King James version has the following translation of St. Matthew's (19:9):
(Text):
Whoever shall put away his wife,-except it be for fornication (Porneia) and shall marry another committeth adultery (Moicheia).
(Translation) :
It is therefore obvious that Christ spoke exactly as related by St. Matthew (19:9), for in the same sentence of the Greek text the words porneia and moicheia are used to express two different thoughts.
But here is another objection: why is the word woman used to mean wife, even in the case of fornication?
The best explanation of this comes from England where, a few years ago, two orphans separated in infancy never met again. One of the orphans took the name of his family of adoption. Later on, the two met, fell in love and were married. They had children and it was later discovered that the couple were brother and sister. So for that reason no existing legislation permitted them to marry. Not having been authorized to marry

legally they had to separate. Having learned the truth, they separated, since any sexual intercourse then became a simple case of fornication, unwitting fornication but fornication nevertheless, due to the fact that they were not really married, since their marriage was void and non-existent. That is undoubtedly the type of marriage that Christ referred to when he said:
Except in the case of fornication.
The Church never recognized divorce, and you have the case of Henry VIII and Napoleon I before whom the world bowed, but not the Church.
The Church has always recognized the invalidity of certain marriages for reasons that made marriage non-existent, but only after an examination, a scrutiny of the facts. The main reason for annulment is refusal or incapacity of consummation, the purpose of marriage being procreation.
I do not recognize that parliament has the right to assume responsibility for dissolving marriage, but parliament does so nevertheless and these words of Our Lord to the Pharisees could very well apply here:
It is for the hardness of our heart (that parliament allows) that you put away your wife, though from the beginning it was not allowed.
The few words placed in brackets are changes needed to apply this to our times.
But the excuse that held good for a nomadic people no longer has any validity in the twentieth century, where we have such a high regard for our own knowledge.
The tragedy of our time is that we have lost sight of the reason for our existence, because of our ignorance of the teachings of the Bible and of the Gospel. We seem to be interested only in our physical welfare; nothing is left for the soul, the only part of our being which has an eternal destiny.
I do not dispute to parliament or to our courts the right to deal with the civil contract in marriage, but no man or group of men has the right to dissolve a legal marriage for any reason whatsoever. Even the Church cannot dissolve a legal marriage. However, on religious grounds, the Church can rule on the validity of a marriage, just as the state can rule on the validity of civil marriage contract.
Those are some of my reasons for objecting to this bill.
There is also a social reason. It must be recognized that the family is the basis of society, that marriage is the cell that safeguards the family, and that if the marriage is broken, the family is destroyed.
How can you expect, Mr. Speaker, that a child raised in an environment where there is no respect for a contract or a promise, how
Proposed Divorce Measures can you expect such a child to harbour the feelings of respect that are due to his parents and elders?
There are two categories of divorces cases:
(a)	between well-to-do people;
(b)	between low income people.
In a divorce between financially secure people, the child is often, if not most of the time, exposed to the little schemes of those idle people who are concerned only with their personal satisfaction, and whose divorce is usually prearranged; and if the father has tried to be strict to teach the child the value of thrift, the suitor, on the contrary, will be generous as a means of gaining the favours of the mother and winning over the child. Such an environment is utterly bad for a child's education, and tends to make him a loafer who will only be a drag on the community.
In the case of persons of limited means, the children, having learned that moral values are meaningless, are an easy prey to juvenile delinquency and early criminality. In both cases, society stands to lose.
The divorce disease-because it is a contagious disease, since the number of cases increases each year to an alarming degree- is common especially among neurotics. At the turn of the century, a study was made on suicide cases in various European countries and it was established that most of those who committed suicide were neurotics.

Here is what Theodore Roosevelt said as reported by Rev. Father Forest, o.p.:
There is a tendency to exaggerate the secondary aspect of public problems, and politicians in particular are prone to busy themselves with questions somewhat important, but of passing importance, in comparison with basic problems. The question of tariff or exchange has literally no importance in comparison with the vital problem of preserving the basic unity of society, that is the family. If husband and wife fulfil their duties towards each other and towards their children according to Christian teaching, we may be sure that the other problems will be automatically solved. If, on the contrary, we have solved the other problems in the most judicious possible way, it will be to no avail if we have lost our national soul; and we are bound to lose it if we cannot place the question of family relations on its true basis.
It is evident that our democratic society is in jeopardy and if we do not acquire this awareness of moral values, we shall be irremediably lost.
Morals are lamentably deteriorating. Devotion to duty does not exist any more; more and more do we look forward to an easy and idle life: less work, more leisure. The god of money has taken precedence over God the Creator. People no longer seem to get bored by spending days, weeks or months of leisure on the southern beaches in wintertime or on ours in summertime. It is a sign of unhealthy idleness. Senses gradually take over the mind. Let us beware.
Let us not forget that several great civilizations have perished because these peoples had lost their sense of values. Each time moral values are deteriorating we are losing ground.
We complain about the communist threat but what are we doing to avoid it? Communist people have an ideal, but what have we got to offer? In the U.S.S.R., work is glorified, praised; studies come first, arts and science flourish. Here, our work is intented to satisfy our sensual desires mainly; work is only a means, not an end to enhance human value. In the arts, the superexistentialists are only trying to create confused sensations or dreams, and these people come in scores.
When Rome came to ask for bread and games and when sexuality had an unequalled influence, bodies and minds weakened and the barbarians had only to reach out to conquer them.
The same thing happened in Egypt, in Persia and in Greece. Despite the admonishments of Diogenes, Demosthenes, Sophocles or Aristotle, the senses took over the mind. Our turn is coming; we are perishing and with us is perishing our democratic civilization.

This sentimentality which leads the hon. member not only to seek the maintenance or the acceptation of the principle of divorce but to ask for broader grounds for it, even in good faith, is undermining our society and accelerating our downfall.
Unless there is a great awakening, our civilization is done for and it will be our own fault.
Reference has been made to divorce courts. The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) has expressed his point of view. Two members, I admit, have made a point of objecting to some divorce bills during the last session because of the frightening number of divorce cases or because of the constitution which makes it easy to get a divorce.
It so happens that the Senate has not enough time to make a thorough investigation of these cases. In some instances, there may be collusion and perjury.
I think it might be well to consider the opportunity of deferring these cases to a court which, at least, would see to it that the Canada Evidence Act is respected and even order the immediate arrest of those who come and commit perjury in order that a divorce be granted.
It is not only a matter of discussing this bill, but also the principle of broadening the grounds for divorce. On this point we, as Christians, and particularly those of us who come from the province of Quebec, must object. We believe there is conflict between civil and criminal jurisdiction, between the provincial authority and the federal authority on this matter.
For all those reasons I have stated, I will vote against this bill.

subtopic: MEASURE TO MODERNIZE DISSOLUTION AND ANNULMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill is another challenge to the natural and divine law, and I think it is an insult to the people of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, before the year 1900, not even a score of divorces were granted in Canada. In 1957, on a national basis, Canada has put through 6,328 divorces and the number of divorced people in Canada, between the ages of 25 and 34 is estimated at 10,000.
We have no reason to believe that this number is going to grow less, on the contrary, it seems due to increase.
To these figures should be added the far larger number of separations, with or without legal sanction.
It is not without reason that divorce is considered as enemy number one of the

family. It can easily be shown as responsible for most of the current problems of juvenile delinquency and others.
Divorce is really a public calamity, and the province of Quebec has always recoiled from opening its doors to such a fearful plague. There are of course divorced people in our province but they had to go outside the province to get their divorce. This does not mean that we do not have our broken homes, and we should not deceive ourselves on that point. It is obvious, though, that the family is held in higher regard in our province.
Listen to this, Mr. Speaker, as regards divorce. One day, it is said, a report was being submitted to the trusteeship council at the United Nations stating that peoples practising polygamy could not have a free government or hope to attain political freedom. Hearing this, the Liberian delegate got up and said: "What difference is there really between polygamy, which permits a man to have more than one wife, and divorce, which permits a man to change his wife as he pleases, or vice versa?"
Even if divorce is quite the fashion across the border, the people of Quebec are justified in considering it as a social evil. Our stand in the matter was forcibly summed up by the former prime minister when he said: Quebec's stand on divorce is clear: we are firmly and irremediably against it.
The Church has always condemned divorce. In his encyclical letter "Casti con-nubii", Pope Pius IX showed all the calamities issuing from that practice, saying in particular:
Divorces cause as many evils as the indissolubility of marriage confers benefits. On the one hand, there is security for the partners in their unbroken vows, on the other hand, the prospect of a forthcoming separation, the possibility of a divorce, make the marriage bond a precarious one. To say the least, they induce suspicions and anxiety
On the one hand, the coming of children, their protection and their education are effectively safeguarded, on the other hand, they are exposed to the most serious prejudices.
Thus, we could not at any time change our attitude in the matter of divorce.
Courts for divorce exist in eight provinces. Two only, Newfoundland and Quebec, have none. Any resident of those two provinces wishing to obtain a divorce must turn to Ottawa for a divorce bill or exceptional legislation.
Proposed Divorce Measures
Since the two world wars, divorces have been mounting terribly, and strong pressures have already been exercised to take those bills out of parliament.
Quebec is right in opposing divorce courts within its territory since it would amount to a recognition and facilitation of divorce. So far, it represents only a concession. Attempts have been made in the past, which continue today, to ease the granting of divorce but, happily, those attempts have failed. I hope that this bill will be nipped in the bud.
The institutions and traditions which are part of our western culture and heritage were based on natural law. We must make our choice. We cannot depart from natural law and at the same time preserve our western and democratic traditions.
Science has advanced, but the multiplicity of divorces brings us back to this decadent period which preceded the fall of the Roman empire: a setback of 15 centuries.
In the eyes of all who look upon the family unit and the children as the basic unit of society, the general welfare of the family and society must be sacrificed to the so-called happiness of the few.
Quebec has never granted a single divorce. This stand is based on natural and divine law as well as on the civil law of French Canada.
In 1867, French Canadians, being irrevocably opposed to divorce, could have hindered the birth of Canada. They wanted the provinces to keep their jurisdiction over marriage.
A compromise was accepted allowing parliament to grant divorce to residents of Quebec by way of exceptional jurisdiction.
To allow the granting of divorce by special legislation enacted by parliament makes for an essential difference, since it leaves untouched the principle of the indissolubility of marriage, and is opposed to the dissolution of marriage by a court which recognizes the right to seek a divorce.
It has been suggested that divorce petitions coming from Quebec be accompanied by the superior court judgment declaring judicial separation on the grounds of adultery. It has even been stated that should parliament legislate to this end, the Senate would then be released from those fastidious inquiries which are causing complaints. After announcement or legislation to that effect, parliament would grant divorces in the province of Quebec on the basis only of a separation for adultery granted previously by a court of the province. Thus, the Senate would be released from hearing these cases but could act upon the judgment ordering separation and upon the preceding enquiry.

Proposed Divorce Measures
This proposal would have the following effect: Parliament would legally and actually entrust to the courts of our province consideration of the divorce cases.
The Quebec judges would act as examining magistrates and the senators and members would only have to give their sanction to measures they had not considered.
We may fear that parliament would very soon tire of passing legislation it would not have considered before and would be inclined to delegate all of its authority to these judges; we would then have those divorce courts which the province of Quebec does not want. Moreover, this proposal would not correct the alleged defect of the present system but merely aggravate it.
The members and senators who already complain they have to pass bills, the merits of which they have neither the time nor the taste to study, would have even more ground to protest if every petition were to be considered not by the Senate committee but by a judge outside parliament.
Under the present system, a Senate committee subdivided in several subcommittees considers the petitions; occasionally, the committee on miscellaneous private bills studies certain cases. The benefit of this procedure is this. While it is true that most members and senators have no time to consider each case according to its merits, the House of Commons and the Senate can at least rely on the integrity of their peers, the members of committees and subcommittees.
I believe that the Senate committee on divorce is by no means inferior to any divorce court in this country.
In 1867, the province of Quebec conceded jurisdiction on marriage to the federal government. This allows parliament to grant divorce bills, notwithstanding the civil code of that province. Now, Quebec objects to the establishment of divorce courts. I hope parliament will never impose the establishment of divorce courts in the province of Quebec.
"The province of Quebec is against divorce", Hon. Arthur Roebuck said a few years ago. He was then, as he is today, the chairman of the Senate committee.
This statement from the hon. senator is true in the case of the vast majority of the population, but still there are too many divorce bills.
It is most regrettable to find among the petitioners a few that are Roman Catholics. Apart from the case where a marriage is invalid according to divine and ecclesiastical laws but valid according to the civil law, I
[Mr. Pigeon.l

see no ground that could justify a petition for divorce.
I cannot accept that a divorce be requested instead of a legal separation-even if a remarriage is not contemplated-to sever, shall we say, all ties with the other party and avoid paying an alimony. In this case, the petitioner is setting a very bad example, for how can one know whether he or she intends to remarry or not.
Today the petitioner denies any such intention, but what about tomorrow. The door is thus opened to many temptations for the other party freed by the divorce, and most probably ill use will be made of the so-called freedom.
But the problem goes deeper still. To say that the bond is completely severed, is to deny and ignore the true nature of marriage, which is an everlasting and unbreakable union in which both "shall be one flesh" (Genesis 2, 24). There are occasions where a separation is allowed by ecclesiastical and civil laws, but the indestructible bond is not altered by such a separation. Therefore it rests with ecclesiastical and civil courts to determine the conditions of that separation.
But, one may say, "my spouse has been unfaithful to me and has committed adultery". Stopping the allowance of your spouse is no way to have the party come back to you and mend his or her ways. On the contrary, it is the way to have your spouse go to anyone. It is to be noted that divorce courts in the other provinces always make a decision as to alimony and property sharing. In Quebec, these questions are decided upon by the courts which grant separation.
There are other means to bring about a reduction in the number of divorces.
In my opinion, one way would be to have more severe rules for the proceedings in the Senate committee. As far as I am aware, but I am no expert and I may be mistaken, the existing regulations do not provide for notifying the third person in a divorce petition. A clause should specify that the third person is to be notified of the hearing of the case. In the present way, a petitioner may charge the other party with adultery with persons unknown, a thing which would be impossible in court.
A short relation of the facts which it would be possible to prove should also be required.
If the committee on divorce needs to take legal opinion on these various points, it should do so.
Moreover, as far as collusion and connivance are concerned, more should be required than a denial, even a sworn denial, on the part of the person petitioning for a divorce.

In most cases, the defendant does not put up a defence, does not even show up, and this is likely to cast serious doubts about collusion, at least by implication. When the defendant does show up, it is to confess to his turpitude. It is disgusting to see the guilty party, and even his corespondent, confess to their misbehaviour. From the legal point of view, it might not be collusion, but something even more disgusting.
That situation is not only peculiar to cases brought before parliament. The same also holds true in respect of divorce courts.
According to the statement made in the House of Commons by Mr. Fernand Girard on January 19, 1956, the divorce reform association of Toronto, in a manifesto urging that the legal grounds for divorce be extended, had this to say:
Did you know that there is divorce by consent in Canada? One judge has said that nine out of ten cases before him are collusive, that is, the parties have perjured themselves in order to get a divorce.
Mr. Girard also referred to an article entitled "Court of Broken Dreams" in the March 1955 issue of Liberty magazine:
A person sat in on a courtroom recently in an attempt to understand why 5,000 Canadian couples annually crack up their marriages in a divorce process of mud-slinging, name-calling and money-wrangling.
Collusion, perjury, make-believe adultery, disgusting details, and all the other evils and scandals deplored by members of parliament and magistrates of divorce courts are inherent in any divorce case, whether it be heard by parliament or by a court.
Complaints are being voiced about it all. It is only logical that the cause-the right to divorce-be removed. At least, we should seek to lessen the evil by insisting on stricter investigations before the Senate committee as well as before divorce courts.
Let us hope that the rules of the Senate committee will be revised and made more rigid. I strongly urge the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) and the attorneys general of the provinces where there are divorce courts, to investigate the procedure followed in those courts.
I am convinced that the Canadian people as a whole will approve any earnest effort made with a view to reducing the number of divorces and to limiting one of the worst evils of society.
For all those reasons, Mr. Speaker, I am strongly against the passage of this bill.

Mr. Speaker, this bill in its implications and purport is of such importance that one could undoubtedly speak at great length upon it. However, I think I can express my convictions and views in a few minutes.
I must say that I have listened with interest and some sardonic amusement to some of the remarks that have been made thus far on this bill. We have heard quotations from the bible in support of divorce, drawing to our attention that the problem existed some 2,000 years ago; that under certain circumstances man and woman should part. Then almost immediately thereafter we heard quotations from the bible against divorce; that it should not be allowed and was not permissible. Therefore apparently, whether we are for or against this bill we can bolster our arguments by statements from the bible; we are safe, no matter where we stand.
I am most certainly in favour of the principles of this bill. A change in the divorce laws of Canada is long overdue. This may not be recognized by some people in some provinces, but I can remember that as far back as 18 years, I think it was, the legislature of British Columbia unanimously passed a resolution asking the federal government to modernize, to christianize the divorce laws of Canada; and if it would not, then to find ways and means of placing the jurisdiction within the legislature of the provinces, at least, as far as British Columbia was concerned.
An honest critique or analysis of the situation existing in Canada as a result of our present divorce law can only bring one to one conclusion; that is, that the effect of the divorce law as it now exists in Canada is such as to condone hypocrisy, collusion, connivance, unhappiness, immorality and perjury. There can be no question of that.
The hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stewart), I believe it was, when speaking on this bill mentioned a couple of clauses in particular and said that in his opinion these would lead to collusion and connivance. How naive can a person get, especially in a statement like that from a lawyer-
He should know.
-who must know that the majority of divorces in Canada today are based on collusion and connivance.
That is wrong; that is nonsense.
Nonsense.

Would the hon. member
permit a question?

My hon. friends say "nonsense". They did not say "nonsense" a few minutes

He was full of nonsense.
That is what a judge said, and I imagine any judge should know.

Mr. Speaker, you will not get a number of members of this house admitting it here, but there are many people who have stated that most divorces are based on collusion, connivance and perjury because of the law of Canada.

I am not bowing to his knowledge or authority, sir. It is too bad that there are so many members who will not face reality and facts.
Why, irrespective of the percentage involved, should a person or persons be condemned to a lifetime of unhappiness, to years of purgatory in their lifetimes in this world, because they made a human mistake and chose the wrong partners? Why, because of a marriage law, when a mistake has been discovered', should people be condemned to unhappiness and a denial of the means to lead a moral life when they do find the person who they think can give them happiness? The present law makes for immorality, it makes for perjury, collusion and connivance because of the very basis on which it works- the only grounds upon which one can get divorce.
I think we all know of case after case where people have got divorces and, afterward, been happy for years and years-cases in which no adultery was ever committed; they were arranged divorces. Why should people have to be put in that position if they are unhappy, if they have made a mistake, if their partners were not what they thought they would turn out to be? Why, we have a situation in Canada where a partner can be committed to a penitentiary for years, or for life as a habitual criminal, or as someone who is incurably insane. Then we say to the remaining spouse: you are tied for life, denied a home life, denied affection, denied love and denied marriage. Surely this does not make sense. Or take the case of a woman who has been deserted by her husband. He has cast off all responsibility and cannot be found. Why should the law say: you are tied, there is nothing you can do about it. Mr. Speaker, that is heathenish. It is unchristian. It is

immoral, and we say that the law of Canada is among the most backward, the most archaic in the democratic world.
As we advance in our thinking on other questions we should advance in this, too. I should imagine that over the years I have received scores of letters from women who have been condemned to loneliness or condemned to immorality because they have to make a choice between obeying the law and establishing a common law relationship since they could not break a marriage vow which had been disregarded. I say the law has taken too much into its hands when it says that this is a condition under which a minority of our people have to continue their lives.
Of course, everyone wants to see a marriage stand and be firm. Everyone wants to see children enjoying the company and protection of both their parents. But when, because of human circumstances, situations arise when separation is best, why should the law say no? One of the previous speakers has mentioned the children. Naturally we are all interested in the children. But speak to psychologists and ask them about the impact on children of an unhappy home, a home where the parents are forced to be together, with all their antagonisms and hatreds. The law says they must.
I think we should use a little understanding. I am not going to mention religion, but the position of the catholics has been referred to. Let me say that this bill in front of us has been based in the main on a statute passed in Australia where a vast number of the people are catholics. So I do not think religion should be brought into this. This question should be appraised on the basis of a feeling of Christianity, of understanding, of realism and of trying to see that the law in its written word does not bring unhappiness and insecurity to men, women and children because it is archaic, stupid, outworn and outdated. All this bill seeks to do is to modernize something which was outdated many years ago.

Mr. Speaker, I think one of my tasks will have to be to set at rest some of the fictions which have been developed during the debate this afternoon and which, if indulged, would present a totally false picture to the Canadian people concerning just what this bill attempts to accomplish.
I think the chief fiction is that we could suddenly make our divorce laws honest by putting into effect this measure or a measure similar to it. That would be a very far cry from what the experience has been in other countries where laws similar to this have

been enacted. I suggest that all the grievances about collusion, connivance and so on would still remain. The broader grounds for divorce would open up new fields which do not exist today and which adultery or the pretext of adultery was never used as a key to unlock in the first place.
May I call it six o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, before the house rose at six o'clock, I was making the point that there were several fictions which surrounded the argument being advanced in support of this bill to broaden the grounds for divorce in Canada, and as I continue my remarks now I intend to deal with them. First, I should like to make it plain, that I do agree that this is an area where some reform is badly needed. While I disagree with what I would like to call the extravagance of the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), I must still confess that, having studied some 1,200 to 1,400 divorce cases presented before parliament in the last four years, or since I have been here, one has to honestly concede that the elements he mentioned of collusion and connivance have entered into them. However, where I do disagree with him and with some of the other hon. members who have preceded me so far in this debate is in their saying that to adopt a measure such as we have now under consideration would put an end to the fictions which surround the only basic ground for divorce, namely that of adultery.
I do not think these fictions would disappear at all, Mr. Speaker; rather, I think we would be simply expanding the field of divorce and that, instead of having a national divorce rate of around 36 per 100,000 of population-and this has been the rate for the last two or three years-we would attain, if we approved such a bill, a divorce rate much higher, well over 40, perhaps into the 50's. I do not say that is necessarily bad, but I think that before we make up our minds on this measure, or on some equivalent measure, we should at least know where we are going.
May I briefly review, against the experience of the 1,200 or 1,400 cases that I have had to consider since coming to parliament the grounds that are suggested in clause 6 of the bill. Perhaps I can make my point even clearer. The ground of adultery is left
Proposed Divorce Measures intact in paragraph (a). Another paragraph deals with wilful desertion. In the 1,200 to 1,400 cases that I have mentioned there have been cases of wilful desertion, and it has occurred for a period of more than two years, so that the ground in paragraph (b) will support the argument of the proponents of the bill.
Another suggested ground is persistent and wilful refusal to consummate the marriage. That would, I think, open up new territory, but not very large. Perhaps it is covered now by the fact that we do also deal with annulments, and I would think that the number of cases would not be altered by the adoption of such a paragraph.
The next paragraph deals with a person guilty of cruelty. That, I think, would open up new grounds. Among the 1,400 cases we have considered in the last four years there have been many instances where a husband or, on occasion, the wife, has been guilty of throwing his or her weight around against the other spouse; but if the cruelty is given a rather exact definition, as is used, for example, in the province of Nova Scotia, the expansion would not be too large.
Another suggested ground is that the other party to the marriage has committed rape, sodomy or bestiality. This would add a few cases to the present number. I have spoken to detectives who have frequently followed the subject for some time, and when they closed in to make the kill or to make the case they have found rather indescribable scenes in hotels and motels. I do not intend to dwell on that except to point out that I think this is a most wholesome addition to any law dealing with divorce reform; perhaps it should be extended to include lesbianism as well.
Another suggested ground is that a party to the marriage has for a period of not less than two years been a habitual drunkard, or been habitually intoxicated by reason of taking or using to excess any sedative, narcotic or stimulating drug or preparation. This I think would open up the field to hundreds of new cases a year; for the experience of the last few years shows that while the petitioning wife-it is usually the petitioning wife who makes the allegations-has told the committee of the other place and the committee of this house about any such errant behaviour of her spouse, this is usually thrown in more or less to create sympathy for her case; but I think these grounds alone would open up the field immensely.
Then, there is a paragraph dealing with frequent convictions for crime. In my experience, at least, I can recall only two cases among the 1,400 where the husband had spent a large part of the married life in

In a companion section immediately following another ground is set forth, namely where the other party to the marriage has been imprisoned for a period of not less than three years after conviction for an offence punishable by death or imprisonment for life or for a period of five years or more. Looking at that clause very quickly it seems to me it is open to abuses, especially in the latter part where it refers to imprisonment for a period of five years or more in that somebody may, inadvertently or advertently, by criminal neglect some night run over somebody with a car under rather drastic circumstances. It might be a first offence and yet the person concerned might wind up with a very stiff penitentiary term. No matter how many people in Canada may desire divorce reform I do not believe they are going to think that a severe sentence for motor manslaughter justifies the breaking up of any marriage at the whim of the party who is left on the outside of the prison walls.
A further ground provided in the bill is having attempted to murder or unlawfully to kill the petitioner. That ground seems reasonable. Fortunately we have not had any cases of that sort before us but I suppose it is simply an extension of the ground of cruelty. Another portion of that clause provides as a ground the committing of grievous bodily harm on the petitioner or the intent to inflict same. That also would be an enlargement of the ground of cruelty, and I think it is a perfect example of the sort of thing one should get at when one enlarges the grounds for divorce to include cruelty.
As we know, in some other jurisdictions the feeding of the wrong type of bird seed to the pet parrot is apt to provoke a family quarrel which can lead to the dissolution of the marriage in the courts, and we certainly want none of that in Canada. By some rewording here I think we could cover the type of cruelty that the hon. member for Timis-kaming (Mr. Peters) has in mind. I would point out again, however, that in my opinion this would enlarge the grounds for divorce and result in many new cases being brought forward that are not covered under our present law. Recalling the experience of 1,200 to 1,400 cases, offhand I can think of very few where strong enough evidence was produced as to justify an allegation of cruelty, so to me this clause would be an expansion.
Then I come to a major and very important ground, wilful and habitual failure to provide maintenance to the other party. A number of cases have come before us where in effect this is what has happened and I


suspect an even larger number where the husband has deserted the wife, for that is the usual circumstance, and has failed to provide for her and the children. Again we get into a rather drastic enlargement, as some people might think, of the grounds for divorce.
A further ground set out in the bill is failure to comply with a decree of restitution of conjugal rights. The number involved there would probably be small. Being of unsound mind and unlikely to recover is set out as another ground, and in that case the person must have been confined for a period of, or for periods aggregating, not less than five years in an institution. I think this is a very wholesome suggestion but we have had no such cases come before us. Again this would enlarge the number of divorce cases.
Yet another clause provides as a ground that the parties to the marriage have lived separately and apart for a continuous period of not less than five years. I think this would also bring forward a large number of cases.
I have made this somewhat rapid survey of the new grounds for divorce set forth in the bill, not to say that the bill is bad, because I think most of it is good, but rather to point out, as I think we must fairly point out if we are to do our duty, that by enlarging the grounds for divorce we are not getting rid of the very many cases of fictitious adultery such as have bothered parliament in recent years.
In his opening remarks the hon. member for Timiskaming used some rather strong words about the present conduct of parliament and its ability to handle divorce cases. I think he made two points; first, that we did not possess the judicial abilities to carry out such chores and, second, that it opened the way to lobbying. If ever any member of parliament stood indicted by words out of his own mouth, Mr. Speaker, it is the hon. member for Timiskaming and his cohort who supports the bill because in the committee over which I have had the honour to preside in the past I have certainly found that members of parliament have been very fair and openminded when they have had to deal with these unfortunate cases. I have also found, however, that there are some members who will be approached by a party to a divorce and will follow that party right down the line until the final vote is taken.
Hon. members will recall that last year the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), who played a large part in these proceedings, informed the house that he was against all divorce cases. If that is so, then that is not a judicial attitude to bring to any committee which is to adjudicate on the rival claims of

two people who have had a falling out because if you come with your mind made up in advance you are certainly not bringing any judicial abilities to bear on these people's problems.
As to the point about lobbying, it is true there was lobbying with respect to divorce cases several years ago and we took the stand that if it continued we would throw out such cases. I think it had a salutary effect until last session when, because of the blockade of divorces, all sorts of people appeared within the gates of parliament to ask that something be done or to present their own particular cases. I think that parliament need not worry about lobbying with regard to divorce cases if we return to the older and sounder practice. However, most of the petitioners who come before us are very poor and they are desperate and when you drive them to the wall so that they do not know whether or not their age old rights are going to be granted you can expect that they will be asking parliament for help, not in the proper way but rather by badgering us with long distance calls, telegrams and letters. This was one of the most shameful heritages of that heroic crusade waged by the hon. member for Tim-iskaming and the hon. member for Skeena last year in that what was a fairly good judicial process was corrupted by then-actions.

We are a democratic country, and if people have no other means of obtaining relief, that is people from Quebec and Newfoundland, then they are entitled to come before us and there are people here who will see that justice is done. May I advert to one other solution of this matter proposed by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters). I think this is one that should be considered. It is certainly a way out of the difficulty. I refer to the question of giving a sort of blanket Canadian domicile so that cases may be dealt with, for example, in the province of Ontario if it is not possible to take action in the province of Quebec. I feel that is a solution that certainly would work out but it has several
Proposed Divorce Measures objections. I believe when we are considering the problem and this solution we should also consider the objections.
In the first place, the supreme court of Ontario and the supreme court of New Brunswick, which would be the two courts that would handle the majority of the cases, would not take kindly to the idea of dealing with some 400 or 500 more divorce cases. It is a solution but I think common sense tells us it would be a very difficult solution to apply.
The hon. member for Maisonneauve-Rose-mont (Mr. Deschatelets), and I think he was supported by one or two other members from Quebec, made the point that divorce should be treated as a provincial problem. I hope that I have understood the point he made, and if not I am sure he will correct me. I will be very happy to be corrected. There are difficulties in that, too, Mr. Speaker. You would have a country in which the inhabitants of eight provinces could obtain divorces and perhaps the inhabitants of two other provinces could not obtain divorces.
I believe we should consider what underlies the fact that the federal parliament is seized with jurisdiction in divorce. When the fathers of confederation sat down to consider this problem they had to devise some workable solution to protect the minorities in the province of Quebec. It was known then and, of course, is known now, that the attitude of the dominant church in that province is that marriage is an indissoluble sacrament. I am not quarrelling with that position at all, Mr. Speaker, but I think it is a fact that has to be considered when we weigh this problem of divorce. Sir John A. Macdonald and the other fathers of confederation seized upon this federal jurisdiction in divorce as one workable solution that would not offend the majority in the province of Quebec and would still protect the rights of the minorities. It may be very easy to suggest that the provinces should be given this jurisdiction in divorce, but I think that if that course were adopted instead of making a forward step we would be going back beyond 1867 itself and the purposes of confederation.
What about the present system, Mr. Speaker? How does it work out? I think ordinarily, under the rules of this house, we should not refer to the people or practices of the other place. However, since there is such a definite connection between what the committee of the other place does and what we do here perhaps I will not be considered out of order if I make some comments. In the first place, I do not think there is any finer judicial mind in Canada than that of my friend in the other place who is in charge

It has been suggested that nine out of 10 of these cases are rigged or the majority of cases which come before parliament are rigged. I think I can make a very simple refutation of that. The national divorce rate, as has been pointed out before, is about 36 per 100,000 people. In the province of Quebec the rate is about 6 per 100,000 people. Perhaps this fact points out how well, under certain circumstances, the move of society to keep the family together can work because I think any province whose divorce rate is one sixth of the national average can point to itself with pride. In the province of Newfoundland the rate is even lower. It fluctuates. One year it may be zero per 100,000 of population and in another year it may be up to one and one half or two per 100,000 of population. By and large, their divorce rate is about 3 per cent or 2 per cent of the national average. Again, I think that is something to which Newfoundlanders might point with pride.
This year, approximately 500 applicants came before us asking for relief. All but about two or three of them were from the province of Quebec. I believe about 90 per cent of these petitioners were women. Of these women, I would estimate most of them were in the humble categories of society. They certainly did not have very much money. Some of them obviously had to save and save for years before they could come to parliament and ask for relief from an intolerable marriage.
I think if we cannot reach agreement here on either broadening the grounds for divorce or taking steps that would rid parliament of an unsavoury job, then at least we can pride ourselves on helping people who really need to be helped. I do not like the handling of divorce in parliament any more than anybody else, and I should like to see us get rid of it, but at the same time there are practical difficulties in the way of taking such a step.
I am not going to be ashamed for one moment of what I have had to do in order to achieve such help for people or of what my colleagues in the House of Commons and in the other place have had to do. This is the highest court in the land and I think any one of us can be proud any time he takes some steps that remove a bit of misery from a person's life.
