rising to take part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, I find some difficulty in view of the amazing nature of this piece of projected legislation. Ordinarily on second reading we are required to keep to the principle of the legislation and to avoid dealing with the clauses in detail. But in this instance so many principles are involved that, in the course of my short remarks perhaps Your Honour will be indulgent enough to allow me to refer to at least one clause in detail.
I can understand how my colleague the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave) felt when he was dealing with divorce suits that come before parliament. I think he had every right to give voice to the things he said but let us remember that this piece of legislation has nothing whatever to do with the divorce suits that come before parliament. This bill is designed to foist upon the provinces of Canada which have divorce jurisdiction certain things they have not asked for. It has nothing to do with those suits that are before parliament. At the outset I should like to make that point clear. This bill has nothing to do except with the provinces which have that jurisdiction.
As to some of the principles involved, there is the matter of jurisdiction which is of importance in the matter of divorce, as is known by all lawyers and by many other people. Then there is the matter of new grounds for divorce. Then the bill takes up the matter of nullity suits. I have always contended that nullity suits are not within the realm of the parliament of Canada because the parliament of Canada was given marriage and divorce. A nullity suit is brought because there was no marriage. If there is no marriage, what jurisdiction has the parliament of Canada to deal with the matter at all?
I do not need to remind the house, particularly the legal members of it, that in the operative clause of a decree of nullity these words always appear: and this court doth order and adjudge this marriage to be and to have been null and void to all intents and purposes whatsoever. Hence there was no marriage. I contend that the parliament of Canada has nothing to do with the matter of nullity of marriage.
Then the bill also takes up the matter of maintenance. I want to deal briefly with one clause of this bill which has to do with jurisdiction, namely clause 4	(1) which
reads as follows:
4. (1) For the purposes of this act, a party to a marriage who is domiciled in any province of Canada shall be deemed to be domiciled in every other province of Canada.

In my opinion, that provision is a draftsman's nightmare. It is like a provision that says, "for the purpose of this act black shall be deemed to be white". It impinges on extremely important questions and on important legal decisions that have been made throughout this country down through the years.
The province from which I come, namely the province of British Columbia, has had divorce jurisdiction of long-standing because the province of British Columbia or the crown colony, as it was then, took the law of England as it existed on November 19, 1958 and that included the divorce and matrimonial causes act of Great Britain. I should like to read the appropriate section from that act. My hon. friends up there in the corner of the chamber can then see that some of the new ground they thought they were plowing is not new ground at all. This is the divorce and matrimonial causes act of British Columbia. It is chapter 97 of the revised statutes of British Columbia, 1948, section 12, which reads as follows:
12. It shall be lawful for any husband to present a petition to the said court, praying that his marriage may be dissolved, on the ground that his wife has since the celebration thereof been guilty of adultery; and it shall be lawful for any wife to present a petition to the said court, praying that her marriage may be dissolved, on the ground that since the celebration thereof her husband had been guilty of incestuous adultery, or of bigamy with adultery, or of rape, or of sodomy or bestiality, or of adultery coupled with such cruelty as without adultery would have entitled her to a divorce a mensa et thoro, or of adultery coupled with desertion, without reasonable excuse, for two years or upwards;-
That was the law of British Columbia and it is still the law of the province of British Columbia, with the exception that because of an amendment made by the parliament of Canada, the wife now has what we call equality of right and can obtain a divorce on the ground of adultery simpliciter without proving adultery with desertion or with cruelty or incestuous adultery. But those added grounds of divorce which are inserted in the projected bill and having to do with rape, sodomy and bestiality are nothing new. They have been recognized for generations by British jurisdictions. That is not new ground at all.
As to the matter of jurisdiction may I say this. I know that in my province-and I am sure the situation is the same in many others-we have built up a great backlog of cases on this matter of jurisdiction in divorce and it deals with that matter not only in substance but in practice. As one great British lawyer once said, in the matter of practice, it is better that the practice be wrong and certain than that it be uncertain.

What result would flow from this bill? One thing I thought might come about is that we might establish in Canada a sort of second Reno. In other words, you can get your divorce wherever you want to go; you can shop around and find the cheapest spot. Possibly a quiet and pretty community like Summerside, Prince Edward Island would be indicated. I know that their court fees are less than ours. That might be a fine place to go and so it becomes Canada's Reno, or some other location. What is going to happen to the courts of that particular province? Are they to be inundated by every man or woman who says to himself or herself, "I can get my divorce more cheaply there and so I am going to go there". We might have two or three Renos over this vast country.
Sometimes it is said-and I have heard it -that the parliament of Canada has never done anything about this matter since confederation. That statement is untrue and it is unfair. The parliament of Canada gave the equal right to the wife shortly after it was brought down in Great Britain. In other words, the wife has the same right as the husband and is under no disability in that regard.
On the matter that was mentioned in this bill about maintenance, the aftermath of divorce which is an extremely serious matter and sometimes an extremely sad and distressing one, may I say this. As a practising lawyer, I have had this happen on many occasions.
The decree of divorce is just one step. Concurrent with that a wife may obtain an order for maintenance. What happens? The husband makes one payment, or two payments, and then he disappears. With us, very often, he disappears to the United States, and then the wife is out of luck. Sometimes he goes to another province of Canada, and if we have reciprocal arrangements with that province, after the expiration of a long time and at the cost of a very considerable amount of money, the husband may be brought to time. But most often this is not the case. Most often it is not the case because the wife has not the money.
I know other lawyer members of parliament must have had the same experience as myself. The procedure of divorce having been gone through this state of affairs arrives and one's client says, "What is the matter with the law of Canada? What is the matter with the courts? Why cannot I get justice?" When it comes to that stage, Mr. Speaker, I simply say this, "Madam, husband and wife are supposed to live together; if they will not live together, the mind of man has not been ingenious enough to find a remedy for

As I said before, so far as parliament is concerned we are debating something here that has nothing to do with parliament. We are debating a bill that seeks to foist something on the provinces of Canada that have this jurisdiction, for which they have not asked. As far as I know, they have not asked for it. They certainly have not asked for it en masse, that I do know.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I find that on no account could I agree to vote for this bill on second reading.

Mr. Speaker, we have before us a legislation which is modestly entitled:
An act to provide in Canada for the dissolution and the annulment of marriage.
The bill might perhaps more aptly be entitled: "Package bill to increase the number of divorces and facilitate their obtention in all provinces of Canada".
For until now, it seems that federal statutes in respect of divorce only contain chapter 85 which provides that:
The law of England as to the dissolution of marriage and as to the annulment of marriage, as that law existed on the 15th day of July, 1870, in so far as it can be made to apply in the province of Ontario, and in so far as it has not been repealed, as to the province, by any act of the parliament of the United Kingdom or by any act of the parliament of Canada or by this act, and as altered, varied, modified or affected, as to the province, by any such act, is in force in the province of Ontario.
That is all I have been able to find in the federal statutes, Mr. Speaker. As far as the other provinces are concerned, with the exception of Quebec and Newfoundland, they already had their own divorce courts before confederation and a special clause of the British North America Act recognized provincial legislation in this matter which already applied before confederation.
The case of the province of Quebec is entirely different, because that province, instead of adopting British common law, was always jealously anxious to keep the French civil code, which does not recognize divorce in any form and, like the Catholic Church, very clearly states that marriage may not be dissolved.
May I be allowed, Mr. Speaker, to refer to clause 185 of the civil code of the province of Quebec which reads as follows:
Marriage may only be dissolved by the natural demise of one of the parties. Marriage may not be dissolved while man and wife are alive.

There can be no plainer or irrefutable statement.
As a Catholic legislator, it is therefore absolutely impossible for me to concur in either the intention or the letter of this proposed legislation, which ignores both Catholic doctrine and the French civil code in force in the province of Quebec.
Catholics recognize only the authority of the Church in matters of marriage annulment. The Church maintains a tribunal which is called the Rota to ascertain the nullity of certain marriages under conditions which make them void in themselves.
While the creed and opinion of members who share neither our faith nor our preference for the French civil code should be respected, it should nevertheless be recognized that the province of Quebec has always refused to institute or to permit the institution by others of civil courts in matters which are not recognized by the civil code. That is why if Bill C-7, now before this house, is adopted, it would constitute an intrusion of a type never witnessed into provincial legislation and, therefore, a most serious breach of the 1867 constitutional act which maintains the French civil code, and recognizes its use in the province of Quebec.
Under section 4, Bill C-7 clearly states:
For the purposes of this act, a party to a marriage who is domiciled in any province of Canada shall be deemed to be domiciled in every other province of Canada.
In other words, this would mean that residents of the province of Quebec would be relieved from the application of the civil code in force in that province and placed under the jurisdiction of divorce courts in any of the eight other provinces of confederation, and without first securing the agreement of the Quebec legislature, which under our constitution is the sole guardian of the civil code. This, in fact, would mean legislating over the heads of the provincial authorities and placing the citizens of two Canadian provinces under the jurisdiction of courts located outside their provinces. What does the Quebec civil code say in regard to domicile? Section 79 specifies that:
The domicile of a person, for all civil purposes, is at the place where he has his principal establishment.
I am pleased to note that this rather unusual suggestion, which is no doubt inspired by a highly developed practical sense, is being put forward by a member of the C.C.F. party, a party which in more than 30 years had never succeeded in establishing a bridgehead in our province before it voluntarily withdrew in favour of the new party. I can understand the sponsor's wish to free the House of

Commons from the strenuous and at times loathsome task of legislating in divorce cases. However, while the intention is excellent, the methods suggested are unacceptable for a number of reasons.
Mr. Speaker, it may be true that divorce bills, whose numbers have been increasing from year to year, clutter up the dominion parliament's order paper, and are perhaps quite tiresome and occasionally give rise to disgraceful scenes. The fact remains, however, that the legislative machinery that has to be put in motion in order to get a divorce in Quebec and in Newfoundland is complicated and cumbersome enough to discourage many would-be divorcees.
There is no need to emphasize the extremely disastrous social and moral consequences for those hundreds of estranged couples who not only live as outcasts of society, leaving a trail of misery and failure, but often leave behind them abandoned and dismayed children who are the unconscious victims of their parents' misconduct. These children are a burden to the community; they are foredoomed to juvenile deliquency and are nearly always found later among the inmates of our reform institutions. Therefore, our laws on divorce will never be strict enough, and not only should we not facilitate divorce, but it is our duty to make it more and more difficult to obtain.
Another aspect of Bill C-7 with which I cannot agree is the list of 14 grounds for divorce instead of one which tradition seems to have recognized so far.
When we take the trouble to read through the evidence given to the Senate committee on divorce, we must admit that often the evidence leaves many questions unanswered and leaves the legislator under the very clear impression that he is faced with a scenario wonderfully played by investigators who are perhaps of good faith, but whom we almost invariably meet in every case.
Bill C-7 tends to establish 13 other grounds for divorce besides adultery. It would be, Mr. Speaker, if you allow me that expression, like supplying 13 other subjects for a scenario in order to vary the procedure and allow a greater number of divorces.
After what I said, it is easy to understand why I am opposed to all forms of divorce and why I feel that most of the divorces granted by parliament are rather sickening. I believe that the best way to settle the question would 90205-6-41$

Nevertheless, the whole question as put forward by the hon. member who sponsors this bill, and by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) who supported him earlier this year, was a procedural one-not that there should be a change in the divorce law but that there should be some procedure for granting divorces elsewhere. The hon. member also mentioned the Toronto case and another case where a corespondent had found her name was used on three or four different occasions. I agree that this was most improper. The person responsible was properly dealt with by the courts and by the law society. But here again this was a procedural matter-it was a case of drawing evidence from the wrong source, false evidence and so on. I submit that the letters sent to the hon. member did not indicate a desire for complete divorce reform in Canada. Cases of perjury, conflicting evidence and so on are, again, procedural matters.
There was a case retried here publicly in the parliament buildings. A great deal of evidence was taken and a great many people appeared here. It ended as a good many other cases do; the committee found difficulty in deciding who was telling the truth and who was not. This is exactly the same situation as occurs when divorce cases are heard before the courts. The court has to decide. A judge sitting alone, or a committee, must decide who is telling the truth. If there is evidence indicating that there has been perjury it should be followed up and prosecution should be undertaken. Again, this is procedural matter.
We must not interpret this artificially engendered outcry as demanding the loosening of the bonds of matrimony to the point suggested in this bill. As I see it, if this bill is carried to a logical conclusion, mental cruelty such as eating crackers in bed or belching at breakfast could very easily develop into the type of divorce case about which we read, laughingly, in other jurisdictions. Cruelty is not defined in this bill as physical cruelty, and in many other jurisdictions the courts have extended the definition of cruelty to the point where they can consider anything which mentally disturbs one of the partners to the marriage as being cruelty. I think you can take almost any marriage in this country and find that kind of cruelty, and if such people wanted a divorce they could get it under the relevant clause in this particular


bill. I am sure that the Rev. Crossley Hunter, who wrote to the hon. member in support of his stand, never intended to support him in connection with a bill which would bring about such results as these.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Is the hon. member not aware that in this clause of the bill there are safeguards? A court would have discretion in establishing protection in the public interest so that the things he has mentioned, such as belching, would never become a ground.

This is more a statement than a question, Mr. Speaker, but I will be glad to answer it. Regardless of how you cut it, this is what the clause says. It is within the jurisdiction of the courts. I have firm faith in the courts of Canada and I would hope that they would never extend this meaning of the word "cruelty", but I do not know. It is very loose. In a few minutes I am going to mention a few other clauses which I think are no better and which, taken together, would open up the whole grounds of divorce to much worse types of collusion than exist today.
I should like to speak about some remarks made by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), and some remarks that I have had to sit here and listen to during the last 11 months. The hon. member for Vancouver East said this afternoon that there is collusion in nine out of 10 cases. He purported to quote some judge who had stated this. I do not know who the judge was, but I know that any judge who made such a public statement could not have been acting in a judicial manner if he felt that a divorce was collusive, but nevertheless granted it. Judges have definite power to refuse divorces, and if any judge has granted divorces in nine out of 10 cases where he thought there was collusion, regardless of who he is, he was not doing his duty.
We can quote all kinds of suspicion. A lot of suspicion has been thrown around. I heard the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) and the hon. member for Skeena make comments about the legal profession. They have stated the legal profession knows that there is this collusion but they have done nothing about it, and when they were called to public account they did not tell the truth. I say that the whole matter of collusion has been blown out of all proportion, having regard to the facts. Those hon. members have refused to accept the words of persons who know and who should know.
Earlier this year I heard the hon. member who sponsors this bill say in this house that the treasurer of the law society did not know what he was talking about. I tried to find the exact quotation, Mr. Speaker, but in the

torrent of words we had during the last session I was absolutely unable to find it, but I sat here and heard that statement. The treasurer of the law society is one of the most respected counsel. His honesty and integrity are above question, and he would never make a statement when he did not know what he was talking about.
I say that the violen and frequent attacks of the hon. members on the legal profession have been most unfair. I say that publicly and now I am going to say one more thing.
I am not a person to stand and accuse, and I make no accusation such as has been made by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Horner), but I point out to hon. members it is a well known fact that when revolution takes place the first people to go are the lawyers. The lawyers are the most vulnerable because they are the people who stand up for the law as it is written, and who believe that the law as it is written must be followed until parliament sees fit to change it.
I am not saying, Mr. Speaker, that there is no collusion in divorce. This would be impractical. I am a practising lawyer; I have handled a good many divorce cases. I think a person can speak better from his own experience than he can from listening to others. I have had dozens of divorce cases and, as far as I recall, there was only one in which I was suspicious that there might have been collusion. The others were absolutely straightforward cases. In most cases the defendants were living together as man and wife in an adulterous state. They were such open and shut cases that one could have no question about collusion whatsoever. I think we have to accept those facts. I think the whole thing has been blown so far out of proportion that we are on the verge of being stampeded into accepting something that is not really there.
Having put the matter into perspective, as I see it, Mr. Speaker, I should like to mention just two principles of the bill. The first relates to domicile and the second to grounds for divorce. There are quite a number of clauses in this bill, but when you break them down these are the two principles. I can see very easily the intent of the hon. member in making domicile a national matter. In doing so, if it were possible-and I am not sure it is-to give a person in this country Canadian domicile, then we would immediately get rid of the problem that is bothering the hon. member and other hon. members relating to Newfoundland and Quebec divorces in this parliament. This would be the first effect because a Quebec resident could come to Ontario and get a divorce and that would be the easy way out.
Proposed Divorce Measures
But I am afraid that is not either legally or practically possible. It cannot achieve its purpose for this reason. Provincial superior courts have jurisdiction only within the province for which they are set up. Under the British North America Act, which is our constitution, section 92, item 14, gives to the provinces exclusively this jurisdiction. I will read it:
14. The administration of justice in the province, including the constitution, maintenance, and organization of provincial courts, both of civil and of criminal jurisdiction, and including procedure in civil matters in those courts.
Now, the judges of the provincial courts are appointed by the governor general, but the courts themselves are provincial. Their jurisdiction is limited within the bounds of the province for which they are set up. If this parliament would legislate that, as the hon. member for Victoria, (B.C.) (Mr. McPhil-lips) said, that black is white, if we would legislate that a resident of Quebec is a resident of Ontario, it would not permit the courts within their own jurisdiction to deal with somebody who is actually in fact a resident of another province. I have heard some hon. members say that the courts would not do it. I imagine that if the courts found they had that jurisdiction they would do it because that is the way the law would read, but I do feel the courts would find that under those circumstances they would not have jurisdiction to try residents of another province in the provincial courts of this province.
Furthermore, another question was mentioned earlier this afternoon, namely international recognition of our courts. It has always been on a high basis, and if we were to change the commonly accepted laws of domicile by an artificial means we would run the risk that some other jurisdiction would not recognize our judgments as being founded on accepted and recognized international principles. I would say that even in Nevada, where in Reno the divorce courts are supposed to have the easiest jurisdiction in the world, people have to go through the formality of going to Reno and residing there to establish residence in that state before any jurisdiction is given to the state. I submit that this could not be accomplished.
In his opening remarks the sponsor of the bill mentioned something else which is at variance with the explanation in the bill and with my understanding of the facts of the matter. He said, as I have it noted here, that matters involving custody of children and maintenance could also be settled by the court granting the divorce. If I understood him correctly this would mean that if a resident of Quebec came to Ontario, brought action for a divorce and was granted a
644	HOUSE OF
Proposed Divorce Measures divorce the Ontario courts would have jurisdiction with respect to the custody and maintenance of the children. I say that this is not the case at all. The courts are still provincial courts. The provinces of this country have been granted jurisdiction over property and civil rights, and custody and maintenance of children definitely fall within these categories. I think the hon. member was mistaken in thinking that a provincial court in Ontario would have anything to do with the custody or maintenance of children in any other province of Canada.
The second principle relates to the grounds for divorce. I do not want to go through them clause by clause for fear of bringing down your wrath, Mr. Speaker, by discussing the clauses of the bill on second reading, but I should like to make a cursory examination of the principles set forth in the bill with respect to jurisdiction and grounds for divorce. The one that bothers me more than any other,
I believe, is the cruelty clause which says that after the other party to the marriage has been cruel to his spouse for one year a divorce can be obtained. In my view that enlarges the grounds too much and I feel that the period of one year is much too short.
Two other grounds provided in the bill are desertion for a period of two years and failure to maintain for two years. I believe these clauses would open the way to worse collusion than has ever been brought to the attention of this house. If desertion for two years were a ground for divorce, how easy it would be for one party to go away for two years, or not even go away at all and for the other party to say in court that he did go away.
The same thing applies to failure to maintain for a period of two years. I think it would open the way to much greater collusion than we have now. In addition, regardless of collusion I think the provision is too easy in any case and opens the way for divorces when grounds are not present. It opens the way for divorces where reconciliation might have taken place. I grant that if after two years people find it impossible to live together another year or two may not help, but there are cases where a situation continues for some time and then something happens that brings the parties together. I found this to be the case a good many times when I was engaged in family court and welfare work. A case will sometimes seem hopeless but then some little thing will happen that will bring the parties together. To provide that cruelty for one year or desertion or failure to maintain for two years shall be grounds for divorce would in my view open up the matter too widely and bring about serious abuses of the divorce laws.


There is also the question of imprisonment. I do not want to go into that in detail. I simply say that imprisonment for a three-year period may be brought about by something for which the party at fault was properly imprisoned but it still may not be the type of crime which would justify the spouse in getting a divorce. It is true that certain types of criminal offences might lead to a divorce but I think that a straight prison sentence should not be a sufficient ground.
The last one I should like to mention is presumption that the other party to the divorce is dead and the granting of a divorce on that ground. This is a situation that has caused many people a great deal of heartbreak in the past. We know of many people who have come to this country and whose spouses, husband or wife, disappeared following the second world war. In many of the iron curtain countries and many of the countries that were overrun the spouse merely disappeared and there is no proof whether he or she is still living or is dead. The other party to the marriage comes to this country and wants to marry. Some jurisdictions in Canada have provided some leeway in this regard.
Under the marriage act of the province of Ontario such a person may apply to a county court for an order presuming the other party to be dead and permitting a marriage licence to be issued, but this does not dissolve the marriage. If by any chance the other party to the first marriage should appear the second marriage is automatically null and void. This provision merely creates a defence against a bigamy charge but does not relieve the parties of their marriage bonds. I do not think we in this country would want to go so far as to say that if a person has disappeared he should be presumed dead and a divorce granted because that person may have done no wrong.
In every divorce action, and I believe this has not been emphasized today, there is a plaintiff and a defendant. The plaintiff must complain that the defendant has done something contrary to the marriage contract. That is the basis for a divorce, a breach of contract, if you wish to put it as simply as that. How can we say that a person who may have been detained beyond his ability to escape, a person who becomes lost, a person who loses his memory or some other such person should be divorced? I think that is going too far. I think we should not extend our divorce laws to the point where a person, having done nothing wrong, may return and find himself divorced.
In fact, I wonder how the jurisdiction of the court would be established. Who would be the defendant in an action of this kind?

It is not spelled out in the bill. Certainly a person who is presumed dead could not be served with any documents and if he is presumed dead he could not even be served by the substituted method of advertising. I do not know what procedure could be adopted, but I think that this final ground for divorce is also wrong in principle.
For all these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I think the bill goes too far. I believe there is some room for divorce reform in this country. There are grounds that should be included in the divorce act, but I feel that this particular bill would not achieve the result the hon. member desires. It would not get rid of collusion. In my opinion it would bring the sacrament of marriage into complete disrepute because as well as being a civil contract it is in most cases a religious ceremony.

Mr. Speaker, if the debate here has proved anything it has proved the great divergence of viewpoints across this country on this most important matter. The views that have been expressed in this house from the various sections of the country are, in some ways, diametrically opposed to one another. I think this should cause us to pause and consider because it is not a matter that can be easily solved nor is it something about which we can reach a rapid conclusion.
The bill before us presents us with a matter of procedure as well as with the broadening of the grounds for divorce. We are discussing today a subject which is of concern to many people for many different reasons. It is of concern to those who are living under the hardships and in a continual state of unhappiness because of broken marriages. It is of concern to those who look after the moral and spiritual welfare of our people. It is of concern to those in the social welfare field who desire stability in family life which is the backbone of our society. There is, therefore, bound to be some conflict of opinion and we have seen this illustrated in the views expressed here today.
I think we should approach this great problem of broken marriages with an open mind, sincerely seeking a far-reaching policy which holds together the family unit, heals the sore spots, eliminates the threatening aspects and instils a sense of responsibility within families so that they will seek to overcome the real hardships. We should not merely find the easy way out for those who will not try to live up to their responsibilities. Reference has been made this afternoon to the biblical injunction, what God has joined together let no man put asunder. However, in this age can we assume that marriages have been joined by God because of an outward ceremony? Unless there is a real
Proposed Divorce Measures acceptance by both parties to the marriage of the will of God there cannot be a real marriage of the heart and soul.
Before we become too strict or rigid in our condemnation of the mistakes in any marriage, let us adopt the attitude of forgiveness that was advocated by Christ himself. Judge not lest you be judged. May I add that, in judging we do not assume we are passing God's judgment. Therefore, let us not ignore the problems which lead to broken marriages. Let us, without prejudice, seek a solution which will take in all points of view.
I think it is easy to understand the view that has been expressed by those who have come from the province of Quebec when we realize the historical origin of the canon law which has taken such a rigid view of marriage. We recall that the canon law developed to fill the gap in civilization after the fall of the Roman empire. The people of that time had seen what had happened to Roman civilization as a result of the lack of respect for marriage and easy divorce. The family law of the Romans, and family life itself, had fallen apart and this was one of the causes of the death of that civilization. We can understand why those who followed took such a strict attitude toward this aspect of life.
Some comments have been made today which tended to cast reflections upon the judiciary in their dealings with divorce actions, and I should like to join with those who have refuted these statements. It is true that allegations have been made that there has been a great deal of collusion in these cases and that perhaps some judges take an easier view than others toward divorce. I do not believe it is fair, merely because there have been some abuses to cast these aspersions upon the whole judiciary which I believe is seeking an honest solution to the problem. I think we will have to agree that as a result of certain disclosures in Ontario punishment has been meted out to those who deserved' it but these investigations did not disclose the widespread abuses that had been alleged.
The bill before us today, Mr. Speaker, deals with four principles: One is the principle oi domicile in Canada in respect to divorce, and it broadens that principle; two, it widens the ground for divorce; three, it widens the ground for nullity; and, four, it provides for a procedure for reconciliation. Although we may not agree in detail with all the aspects of this bill I think it has proved to be a good vehicle for an honest discussion and study of this problem. There are many things in it that are worth considering.
In so far as the first principle is concerned the matter of domicile, it has been dealt
646	HOUSE OF
Proposed Divorce Measures with fairly adequately today but I should like to make some comments in respect to one or two aspects of it which I do not believe the sponsor of the bill intended and for which perhaps safeguards should be put in the bill. I feel that the widening of the domicile would entail certain difficulties. This provision would assist those in the province of Quebec or the province of Newfoundland which do not have a court in which to apply for a divorce, and such people could go to the province of Ontario, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick or Prince Edward Island. This would place a very unfair burden on these other courts if they had to deal with a large volume of cases coming from these provinces. I suppose the sponsor of the bill feels this would be preferable to having these people come to the House of Commons. However, I would point out that in giving these courts jurisdiction to hear these cases he gives them no greater power than we could give to the exchequer court.
He cannot, by extending this domicile which can only be effective with respect to divorce, give to other provinces like Ontario the power to deal with property and civil rights within Quebec or Newfoundland; nor could they deal with the custody or the maintenance of children or the maintenance of the petitioner. This would be a matter that would have to be settled in the province of domicile, because there is no such thing as domicile in Canada which is recognized in law. This is only a vehicle to add jurisdiction to the courts for a particular purpose and may not be recognized by other courts outside Canada under the conflicts of law.
There is one abuse that could happen and I do not think it was indicated. A husband living in New Brunswick or in Prince Edward Island could, if he wished to do so, go to British Columbia and bring an action for divorce against his wife. The poor wife would be put to the expense of having to defend that action in a court in British Columbia and the cost to her would be almost prohibitive unless she was a person of means. That is something that would have to be safeguarded if that extension of domicile were to be carried out.
The other principle dealt with is the matter of broadening the grounds for divorce. I think it is fair to say that there are in Canada today many people who realize that the grounds for divorce are too restrictive. There are many who feel that there are grounds that could be permitted. However, in their thinking they are disturbed and perplexed as to what limit may be placed on these grounds so that there is not, on the part of the couple being married, an inclination to say, "If we cannot get along, we will go and have our 

marriage dissolved". The grounds, whatever they may be, must be strict enough to put each couple on their mettle to make an honest attempt to make a go of their marriage. Marriage is a partnership. The sooner the couples concerned realize that fact, the fewer difficulties we shall have in dealing with the matter of divorce.
I will not go into the particulars set out but if I wanted to be facetious I could find the opportunity. There is one clause which states that if one of the parties has been a habitual drunkard for a period of two years or has been otherwise intoxicated, there would be grounds for divorce. One could perhaps say that a nagging wife could drive her husband to drink and then, after a period of two years, could divorce him. However, I do not think the sponsor meant that. However, as I said, it is difficult to draw the line between the desire, on the one hand, to relieve the hardships of those who made a mistake and are suffering and, on the other hand, the desire to be strict enough to force people to live up to their responsibilties.
Within the last few years a royal commission in England has been dealing with this problem of having the divorce laws extended and the experience in dealing with those extended laws. The commission has been reporting since 1955. I should like to read one or two of the paragraphs from their findings. It might help with some of the principles involved here. At page 24 of the Reports from Commissioners, Inspectors and Others, volume 14, "Marriage and Divorce to Minor Offences", volume XXIII, paragraph 69 (i) we find the following under the heading "Views of those nine members who are opposed to the introduction of the principle of break-down of marriage"; that is, I presume, where a marriage is considered to be completely at an end, there should be a divorce perhaps by consent. I quote:
69. (i) We have rejected the introduction into the law of the principle that a marriage should be ended if it has irretrievably broken down, because, as we show later, in whatever form that principle might be introduced it would entail the recognition of divorce by consent. In its more fully developed forms it would also entail the recognition of divorce against the will of a spouse who had committed no recognised matrimonial offence. It is the introduction of either of these elements that we regard as fundamentally objectionable and as containing the seeds of grave damage to marriage as an institution.
(ii) We believe that the consequences of providing the "easy way out'' afforded by divorce by consent would be disastrous to stability in marriage. The inevitable result would be the granting of divorces in cases where no real necessity for the remedy had arisen. In other words, the divorce rate would be swollen by the failure of marriages which would otherwise have held together with advantage to both parties as well as to children. People would then come to look upon marriage less and less as a life-long union and more and

more as one to be ended if things begin to go wrong, and there would be a very real risk that in the end widespread divorce would come to be an accepted feature of our society. As those attitudes spread they would undermine, and ultimately destroy, the concept of life-long marriage.
(iii) The evils which would result if the community were to come to accept divorce as the obvious way out of all marriage difficulties need no elaboration, save in one respect-the consequences for children. We were enjoined to pay special attention to the "interests and well-being of children". We are deeply concerned about the effect on children of the present divorce rate: their suffering would be multiplied if divorce were to become more widespread. The best home for children is of course a happy home, but in our opinion (and most of our "expert" witnesses confirmed this) children can put up with a good deal of friction between their parents so long as the home remains intact. The relations between the parents must usually be very bad indeed before a divorce is in the interests of the children.
Then in paragraph (vii) they go on to state as follows:
(vii) For the reason given in paragraph 38 we refrain from any discussion of the religious aspect of marriage. Apart altogether from this aspect, we believe that it is fundamentally incompatible with the concept of marriage as a union for life for the parties to be free to put an end to it by agreement. It seems to us self-evident that a marriage cannot be the concern only of the partners to it. If there are children, their interests must be considered. But whether there are children or not, the state must be concerned in the maintenance of a marriage and in its dissolution, because the state has an overriding responsibility to ensure, in the interests of the community, that the institution of marriage is upheld. For marriage is not merely a civil contract between the parties to it. It is a status arising out of that contract and, as a status, it concerns the community as well as the parties. If husband and wife were free to terminate their marriage at pleasure, then marriage would become a purely contractual relationship and the interests of the community would receive no recognition.
The royal commission made certain suggestions after their study which they considered possible for increasing the grounds for divorce. One suggestion was as follows, and in connection with this suggestion 18 members were in favour and one member was against it:
(1)	The present law of divorce based on the doctrine of the matrimonial offence should be retained.
(2) (Nine members in favour). The principle that a marriage should be dissolved if it has irretrievably broken down-as exemplified by divorce by consent, divorce at the option of either spouse after a period of separation, or divorce on a comprehensive ground of break-down of marriage-should not be introduced into the law.
(3) (Nine members in favour). There should be provision for divorce in cases where, quite apart from the commission of a matrimonial offence, the marriage has broken down completely; accordingly, where husband and wife have lived separate and apart for a period of at least seven years immediately preceding the application, it should be possible for either spouse to obtain a decree dissolving the marriage, provided that the other spouse does not object.
(4)	(One member in favour) -
Proposed Divorce Measures
This was a minority suggestion:
A marriage should be indissoluble unless, the spouses having lived apart lor not less than three years, either spouse shows that the facts and circumstances affecting the lives of the parties adversely to one another are such that it is improbable that an ordinary husband and wife would ever resume cohabitation.
There were also other suggestions that are somewhat similar to the suggestions set out in this bill. Mr Speaker, I think that considering the results of a royal commission that has studied this problem in a country that has laws similar to ours-in fact, our laws originally evolved from that country- a country that has widened its divorce laws, we should take some cognizance of the findings it has made. We should give some consideration to the findings of the royal commission in our study of the problem. The royal commission has suggested areas in which grounds for divorce could be safely extended.
In passing, I think one could say that if a great deal more attention were paid in the preparation for marriage there would be less trouble after marriage. I think it is fair to say that certain churches, including the Roman Catholic church, the Jewish church, the United church and some others, are seriously studying this problem and are taking up programs of trying to inform young couples before marriage of their responsibilities. I trust and hope that all those who are interested in this problem will continue to make greater efforts in providing these preventive methods so that we will have less cause for divorce.
I wish to say one word, Mr. Speaker, in respect to the procedural aspect that is dealt with in this bill. I think that as far as the eases that come before this House of Commons are concerned, most of us are in agreement that we have not the proper procedure. But in the over-all procedure I think that, even as dealt with before our provincial courts, greater attention must be given to the aspect of reconciliation mentioned in this bill.
We have read and noted the success in some of the states of the United States, where if one party to a marriage voluntarily goes to the court and states his or her problem the court can then summon the other spouse and discuss the problem. They have reported that they have been able to save as many as 50 per cent of these marriages. After they bring the couples together they have them sign a marriage contract, acknowledging in writing their various responsibilities. This has done a great deal to impress upon these couples their responsibilities in marriage.
In our larger centres in Canada we have family courts which are doing a great job. Perhaps this work could be extended to

Proposed Divorce Measures other centres. I feel that the time has come when most of the married couples coming to courts for divorce should be required to go through a procedure to ensure that all efforts are made to see whether reconciliation can be obtained. Through the assistance of marriage counsellors, the assistance of clergymen and others, a great deal more could be done in the matter of rehabilitation and reconciliation of married couples. I think this is a matter which could very well be the subject of study before we come to final consideration of any grounds for extending divorce. I feel it would be one of the safeguards in preventing any further collusion on extended grounds for divorce. If one could feel that where a marriage has been in difficulty and in danger of breaking up it has gone through a set procedure to ensure that every effort has been made for reconciliation, then I think we could feel safe in dealing with the extension of the grounds for divorce. I think that should allay the fears of those who do not believe in the granting of divorce.
I would like to say on this matter of procedure and, yes, even on the matter of grounds for divorce, that divorce cannot be settled by blackmail or sit-down strike methods by any minority group, imposing its will upon others by threats or obstruction. Nor can it be solved by the inaction of others. There must be a realization of the problem. I think in all fairness-and I take the risk of saying this-there must be a realization by those who oppose divorce that a large number of people do believe there are grounds for divorce. Although these groups have the right to enforce their views on their own members-that is, members of churches -they should adopt a tolerance which would permit a reasonable extension of the divorce law and a proper procedure to deal with such cases, especially by those who do not belong to their group.
I plead that we face up to the problem; that we study it and come to a logical solution based upon the social and moral needs of our society.

Mr. Speaker, this is one of the most important pieces of legislation that will come before this house this session and I want to congratulate the hon. member who has introduced it. There are a great many items in the various clauses of the bill with which I am not in entire agreement, but in the general principle of broadening the grounds for divorce I am in entire agreement. I am sure that some of those items in various parts of the bill which do not meet with my approval or the approval of other members can be remedied if the
measure should go before a committee. I should just like to let the hon. member know that if we ever get to a vote on this bill this evening I intend to support it.
I have no intention of following the hon. member who introduced this measure with reference to his actions last session. He took a certain amount of credit to himself for blocking divorces, but I deplored his action at that time and I still do. I think he was wrong in the attitude he took. However, I am in favour of broadening the grounds for divorce.
This is not the first time a bill for enlarging the grounds for divorce has been introduced into this house. I think it was in the thirties that the present leader of the government in the other place introduced a bill with this object in mind. In 1937 a bill was introduced in the other place by the Hon. Senator Mc-Means from Manitoba, and the present leader of the government seconded that measure which received the approval of the majority of the members of the other place. Nevertheless, it was rejected by the House of Commons.
At the time the bill was introduced, an editorial appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press. I do not always agree with everything the Winnipeg Free Press has to say in its editorial column but this was one occasion on which I found myself in agreement with that newspaper. On March 10, 1938, referring to this bill which was introduced in the Senate by Senator McMeans, the editor said:
There are very sufficient reasons why the rigidity of the divorce law should be relaxed in Canada as it was last year in Great Britain, the situations in the two countries being largely similar. It is a subject on which there is, of course, great difference of opinion, and it is important that in the discussion of the bill introduced by Senator McMeans there should be calm consideration of the whole situation. At present, divorce can be granted only for adultery or the committing of unnatural offence. There are many Canadians who believe there are other valid grounds that should be recognized and that more harm than good results from not doing so.
The importance of the home as the basis of our national life and the consequent need of preserving the marriage bond as inviolate as possible may be fully conceded. There is no intention of loosening that tie beyond the requirements of sound and necessary consideration. To do so would be to seriously increase many of our social problems closely related to family life. But entirely unreasonable and unwholesome conditions are resulting from the refusal to grant divorce except for practically only one cause.
If a worthless husband deserts his wife and goes off to the United States and lives there permanently, she is condemned under the present law to a life of, loneliness for the rest of her days. The same thing results if either husband or wife becomes incurably insane. Because one life has been fatally blighted, should the other be sacrificed to an undue degree? If a sailor is missing and never returns, must his wife be denied a normal life? If a brutal

husband Is persistently cruel, must the wife endure it with no hope of release? If there is no natural affection, is there a home worth preserving?
So much for that. I do not think the sponsor of this bill has any intention of broadening the grounds for divorce to the extent which has been suggested by some hon. members; I certainly do not think they will be as wide as they are in certain states of the North American continent-I will not refer to any particular state for fear I may make things more difficult for the minister of external affairs. The fact remains that we are far behind the United Kingdom in this matter of the divorce laws. The United Kingdom widened the scope of its divorce laws in 1937. The sponsor of the bill on that occasion was, I believe, Mr. A. P. Herbert, the author of a famous book-I am not sure whether it is called "Holy Deadlock" or "Unholy Deadlock". I believe that is a takeoff on wedlock.
In the course of today's debate there have been some references to holy writ. I have no intention of putting on the record the various chapters and verses to which reference has been made, but for the benefit of some hon. members who are perhaps not as well acquainted with the holy scriptures as you and I, Mr. Speaker, I should like to give the references so that if any of them wish to look them up they may do so:
St. Matthew, 19th Chapter, verses 3 to 9 St. Mark, 10th Chapter, verses 2 to 12 St. Luke, 16th Chapter, verse 18 St. Paul, First Corinthians, 7th Chapter, verses 10 and 11.
I am not sure of the other. I think it is St. Paul's epistle to the Ephesians but, as I say, I am not so sure of that, and you may have to correct me, Mr. Speaker. I think it is Ephesians, Chapter 5, verses 31 and 32.
Mr. Speaker, this question came before the House of Lords in Britain. As I mentioned, the bill was passed in 1937. However, a royal commission had been appointed to deal with the matter as far back as 1907 and it was not until 30 years had passed that the views of that royal commission were expressed in the statute law. In 1930 the question was debated in the House of Lords. A bill was introduced, and one of the speakers in the debate was a gentleman with whom you are very well acquainted by name, if not personally, that is, Lord Birkenhead, who was formerly Sir Frederick E. Smith. Lord Birkenhead had adorned the English bar for a great many years and in speaking in that debate he said, referring to the history of the legislation:
In my view the history of the matter has very great importance. The act of 1S57, far too late in
Business of the House
my view, removed a jurisdiction from the ecclesiastical courts which-I say it with all respect- they were ill-fitted to discharge. Their view was that marriage was and ought to be indissoluble. The ecclesiastical courts themselves, who laid down this doctrine with every circumstance of canonical formality, prayed in aid a number of fictions under the head of nullity which were comparable to the chicanery which disfigures our lav/ today. I pass by the conjugal eccentricities of Henry VIII with the observation that they met with a good deal of indulgence from the ecclesiastics of that day, and I come to the latter part of the seventeenth century. Towards the end of the seventeenth century it was recognized that, by the procedure of a private Act of Parliament, divorce ought to be obtainable on the ground of adultery. It is hardly necessary to say, having regard to the age with which I am now dealing, that this was a method of relief which was open to the rich and open to the rich alone, and it is a great reproach to our institutions over so long a period of time that when once it was recognized that divorce ought to be conceded on the ground of adultery a dividing line should have been drawn between rich and poor.
Ten o'clock.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I inquire what the business is to be tomorrow and Monday?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Tomorrow we shall continue with the second reading and, I hope, the committee stage of Bill No. C-49, respecting technical and vocational training assistance. In view of the importance of this bill it is likely to take most of the day, and there is a private members' hour from five to six. However, should there be any spare time, I suggest that we consider setting up three special committees, namely item No. 8 on the order paper, leading with the procedure of the house; item No. 11, dealing with Indian affairs; and item No. 9, which has reference to research.
On Monday, if Bill No. C-49 has been disposed of, we will go on with the resolution concerning the productivity council. If that is completed during the course of the day, we will take the resolution dealing with veterans pensions. Tuesday would be a continuation of those two measures in whatever stage we have reached; that is, second reading of the bills, and perhaps the same for Wednesday. Therefore, on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday we would be dealing with the productivity council and veterans pensions legislation. If the house makes rapid progress on Monday and Tuesday we might start with supplementary estimates on Wednesday.
It being three minutes past ten o'clock, the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
